utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, there is nothing indicating that, because the Prosecution brief was filed on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At 5.00, Your Honour, one hour after deadline. That's number one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean the deadline for the registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But why I'm putting that on the record? Because on the cover sheet of the Prosecution brief, there is a time, 5.00 p.m. The normal, regular office time, working time of the registry, is until 4.00 p.m. So what I'm saying -- because I was informed, Your Honour, that they're asking for a six-hour extension, and I was really favourable to that. No problem. It happens. Things happen. But at that time, I was of the opinion that my brief should be guarded with the armed officers because I didn't want to have any possibility that my brief, through any channels, will go into those hands. And Ms. Atanasio was very, very kind, very professional, and she told me that she will keep my brief in her office, and once the Prosecution brief will be filed, I will get their copy and they will get my copy. So just for the record, I again would like to express my gratitude to the professional work of the registry, and also to put on the record the fact, because on the cover sheet which is the part of filing of Dr. Simic brief, there is a time 4.15 p.m., due to the probably technicalities in transferring from Ms. Atanasio's office to the registry main office. Because I want everything to be proper and fully in accordance with the Rules. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there anything the Prosecution would like to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just this: I don't know where the 10.00 p.m. comes from. As Your Honour rightly points out, we filed it at 5.00. UN working hours are 9.00 to 5.30. The registry says 4.00 p.m. The registry, if you arrange in advance, will accept things up to 5.00 or 5.30, if you ask them. And we did so. We were having a formatting problem and filed at 5.00, and we certainly didn't see Mr. Pantelic's brief until I think much later that day or the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber finds no substance in all these submissions regarding the time of filing, and also there's no reason to doubt the integrity of the registry staff at any time when any documents are being submitted as to how they are going to be handled, the staff are always handling any documents that are filed professionally. So we'll start our closing arguments with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution is grateful to you for permitting us this opportunity to address you orally today. To assist you, can I provide you with an outline of submissions which will basically set out the manner and the content of what we intend to present to you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: You will see on that brief outline of submissions, there are a number of topics that we will cover. We propose to split the submissions between Mr. Re, Mr. Weiner, and myself. Mr. Re will commence the closing submissions and will deal with points 1, 2, and 3 on the -- indicated on the outline. I shall deal with point 4, and Mr. Weiner will deal with point 5. That will leave the issue of sentencing, which we will no doubt get to this afternoon, and we will discuss that and make arrangements for someone to -- one of us to address you on that particular issue later this afternoon. But essentially, that's the manner in which we will conduct the closing submissions. So Mr. Re will commence on points 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Di Fazio, for this outline. It makes it easier for us and I'm sure for the other parties, to follow the arguments. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours have heard a lot of evidence in the 20.000 pages of transcript and the hundreds of exhibits which have been tendered in the length of this long trial against the three, formerly four, accused. I start with the term "ethnic cleansing." It's a term which has been used by many of the witnesses. It's a term which isn't really legally defined, but it is one that everyone has understood for many years in relation to what happened in the former Yugoslavia. The definition, the first and best definition, one which cannot really be improved upon, is that of the Special Rapporteur, who reported, in 1992, defining ethnic cleansing in his report of the 17th of November, 1992, which the Defence put into evidence. That's Exhibit D2/2. He defined it as: "the elimination by the ethnic group exercising control over a given territory of members of other ethnic groups." In a nutshell, that's another way of describing persecution, as a crime against humanity, or as legally defined, persecutions as a crime against humanity. It's another way of describing in a nutshell what happened in Bosanski Samac from the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, until the end of the indictment period, the 31st of December, 1993, during which a municipality which had formerly had a non-Serb majority and which people had lived together of the three ethnicities - Serb, Muslim, and Croat - for many years, and the situation was dramatically changed in that period until there were almost no Muslims or Croats left. In fact, Bosanski Samac is an interesting case in the history of this Tribunal, and in the context of the other cases which have been heard here, and the findings in other cases of the persecutions which occurred in Bosnia -- across Bosnia-Herzegovina over the years. It is a case which really encapsulates most of the things. It's a localised version of the larger ethnic cleansing or persecutions which occurred throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the indictment period. It really is, to summarise, a textbook, classic, localised case of ethnic cleansing. It's almost a case in which you can tick the boxes as to what to do if you were to eliminate an ethnic group from a territory, that is, if the ethnic group exercising control was to eliminate another ethnic groups or groups from its territory. So what do you do? Well, first, first you need a takeover, or the imposition of some form of military control, exercised with a discriminatory intent. Because without that, there is no ethnic cleansing. You cannot put your plans into action. You need civilian authorities, new civilian authorities, acting with the military, to take control of the territory. You then need to "encourage," for want of a better word, the members of other ethnic groups to want to leave the territory. There are various ways of doing this. You could do it by force or you could do it in such a way as to make life completely unbearable for the minority -- for the ethnic groups which are under control, and they are basically forced to leave. So you can tick the box of the takeover. You can then declare it a state of emergency, tick that box. Imposing a new form of repressive and discriminatory government and control over a formerly democratically elected municipality. What next? Arrest your political opponents. On what basis? Spurious, discriminatory political grounds, ethnic grounds. You can use them for propaganda purposes. You can interview them almost at gun point and use them on -- in radio and television interviews, for your own propaganda purposes, to denigrate these people who have no choice in the matter. That's another box that could be ticked of what happened at Bosanski Samac. And of course, you can arrest all males of military age, again on discriminatory, persecutory grounds, only because of their ethnicity, and imprison them. And then when you imprison them, without resort to the rule of law, and in a very extrajudicial manner, you imprison them in the most inhumane conditions, in which you allow torture, sexual assault, and murder. And this new system put in place by the new authorities, civil and military, allow this to occur in their own detention centres, municipal and military. That's another box you can tick as to what happened in Bosanski Samac. Having isolated the male members of the other ethnicities from their own -- from their families and their homes, their community, what do you do with the females and the elderly, especially if your detention centres, your makeshift detention centres, are full? Well, you isolate them somewhere else. You use the police to take them to compulsory isolation, away from their communities. What else? What are the other similarities? What are the other boxes you tick? Well, as in other municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you allow vicious, psychopathic, Serbian paramilitary thugs to terrorise the civilian population. You allow them to run amok. You allow them to institute and continue a reign of terror against people who have committed no crime, other than to belong to a different ethnicity. Another box you can tick as to what happened at Bosanski Samac. All the while this is happening, the new municipal authorities issue discriminatory decrees, orders, and legislation aimed directly at the other ethnicities, orders preventing more than three of the other ethnicity from congregating, orders that non-Serbs should wear white armbands, orders prohibiting non-Serbs from leaving the territory. Another box that can be ticked. And what's another one? Another one is the use you make of your ethnic opponents, for want of a better word, in putting them to work for you. Using non-Serbs as fodder to do your forced labour in the most inhumane conditions, exposing people to the most inhumane forms of working conditions, sending people to the front line to dig trenches while bullets are whizzing over their heads. If that isn't designed to make people want to leave a municipality, the Prosecution doesn't know what could be. And in the most cynical use of these people for forced labour, what else could you do? What other box could you tick? Well, it's the plundering and looting of your ethnic opponents, property and homes, where you use Muslims and Croats to loot, to systematically loot and steal property that could be in no way legitimised by an armed conflict. Going through houses and cleaning them out of people's belongings and shipping them off to Serbia or using them as the Crisis Staff directed. But what was all this -- what was all this directed to? And this is the main box you tick, and that is the ultimate aim of the joint criminal enterprise to persecute in Bosnia, and that is the ethnic cleansing, the deportation, the removal of the non-Serbs from their homes, from the municipality. All of those things for which you can tick the boxes of the ethnic cleansing lead to that one thing, and that is the removal of these people from their territory and to do so, you needed to do the other things I've outlined first. You need to create a cache of people you can trade, because that's what it was, people trading, a cache of people you can imprison and hold there in your holding centres for use in trading of people like cattle with the other side. Those are the people in detention. For those outside of detention, you tick the box of making living conditions so unbearable that they are forced to leave, and people are given a quick way out through an exchange or they are forced to remain and bear the intolerable and inhumane conditions created by the new authorities in control of the municipality. And that, Your Honours, is what we say -- is why we say that Bosanski Samac presents a classic, minuscule example of the horrors of what occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the indictment period. I turn to the joint criminal enterprise, which is charged in the indictment. Your Honours will of course be aware, from reading the indictment and reading our submissions and of those of the Defence, especially Dr. Simic, that the words "joint criminal enterprise" are not actually used in the indictment. However, the indictment describes what occurred in paragraph 11 as the three accused "acting in concert together, and with other Serb civilian and military officials, planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetting...persecutions in -- of Bosnian Croat, Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians on political, racial, or religious grounds, throughout the municipalities of Bosanski Samac, Odzak, and elsewhere in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." The Prosecution, of course, acknowledges that the indictment is slightly unusual in the way it has charged the persecutions or the joint criminal enterprise against each of the three accused in that it has charged all three, in paragraph 11, with complicity in the same common purpose or joint criminal enterprise, whereas in paragraphs 12 -- sorry - paragraphs 13, 14, and 15, it has named each of the accused separately. And the way it's charged is the underlying acts which the Prosecution relies upon in paragraph 12 to prove the method of implementing the persecutions are almost the same in relation to paragraphs 13, 14, and 15, with the addition of an additional underlying act for Dr. Simic in paragraph 13, that is, B, the issuance of discriminatory decrees, and Mr. Zaric, in paragraph 15 of paragraph D, the interrogation of Croats, Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians and forcing them to sign false or coerced statements. The Prosecution's submission is the Trial Chamber should consider each of the four separate methods there of charging the accused as being basically the same and one in relation to the same common purpose or joint criminal enterprise to persecute. Now, Dr. Simic, in his submissions, raised an issue at -- I take Your Honours to paragraph 658 to 659, that is page 226 to 7 of Dr. Simic's submissions, in which he directly refers to the failure of the Prosecution to "plead a joint criminal enterprise in this case, denying Dr. Simic notice and a fair trial." The Prosecution simply deals with this in this manner. Unfortunately, during the editing of the Prosecution's final trial brief, a footnote dropped out. It was a footnote which was supposed to refer to the case of the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic, Sainovic, and Ojdanic, a decision on Dragoljub's Ojdanic's motion challenging jurisdiction, joint criminal enterprise of the 21st of May, 2003. The Prosecution assumes that Dr. Simic's counsel was unaware of this decision, which was -- which only came down a few weeks ago when he wrote his submissions. That case, the Appeals Chamber basically has dealt with the issue of the meaning of joint criminal enterprise as opposed to common purpose, and at paragraph 36 of that decision, the Appeals Chamber held: "First concerning the terminological matter raised by the Defence, the phrases 'common purpose' doctrine on the one hand, and 'joint criminal enterprise' on the other, have been used interchangeably and they refer to the same thing. The latter term - joint criminal enterprise - is preferred, but it refers to the same form of liability as that known as joint criminal enterprise." And that's the decision of the five Judges of the Court of Appeal. His Honour Judge Hunt appended a separate opinion in which His Honour actually gathered all the different terms which have been used in the Tribunal's history and in its jurisprudence to describe the same thing, including common design, acting in concert, common purpose, and, of course, joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution's submission is it is simply a terminological shift over the years, arising from its first use in the Tadic appeals judgement in which the Tadic Appeals Chamber itself used several different terms, seemingly interchangeably, common design, common purpose, complicity, and joint criminal enterprise. In the Prosecution's submission, nothing at all turns upon the use of the words, and this indictment confirmed many years ago of the words "acting in concert together." It simply means complicity in a joint criminal enterprise, the joint criminal enterprise being to persecute. The Defence have been well and truly on notice of the joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose, or the common design the Prosecution has alleged against them in the pre-trial brief, in the Prosecution's opening, in the evidence as it has unfolded, and of course in the Prosecution's response to the 98 bis motions of the Defence for acquittal, in which the Prosecution used the term "joint criminal enterprise" interchangeably with "common purpose," thus reflecting the terminological shift in Tribunal jurisprudence. While on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If you excuse me, Mr. Re. I understand that your submission is that there is no difference in substance between what is said in the chapeau in paragraph 11 in the indictment, where the words "acting in concert together" are used, and in the expression or, well, "joint criminal enterprise." You mean that they are covering exactly the same things; it's only a different use of words? This is what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I mean, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Why did you find it necessary to change the expression and not go on using the same words as in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my submissions now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No. In your reply on the 27th of September, and even in your final brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because by that stage there had been a terminological shift which was occurring in Tribunal jurisprudence, culminating in the Appeals Chamber decision of the 21st of May this year, in which the Appeals Chamber finally expressed its preference for the use of that term. The Prosecution could see it coming because it had been used in a number of different cases and a number of different indictments. We just wished to make it completely clear that it meant acting in concert. So it could fit in, whatever we said here would fit in with the evolving Tribunal jurisprudence of the meaning of complicity in a criminal -- under Article 7(1) of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I may continue. One could get the impression that the words used in the chapeau paragraph 11 indictment so to say limited in time what was made by the three accused, what they planned and what they, so to say, decided, shared the intent and so on, starting from a certain point of time and then going forward, whereas the joint criminal enterprise seems to be stretching its effects and having its roots further back in time. Do you see any difference there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The way the Prosecution approaches it is that there was at the time, at the commencement of the indictment, a joint criminal enterprise in operation in Bosnia-Herzegovina to persecute non-Serbs. It's an enterprise which the accused may join at different points and in a different manner, and the words in the indictment, in paragraph 11, refer to acting in concert together with other Serb - that is, unnamed - Serb civilian and military officials aiding and abetting. It's referring to their participation, acting in concert with these other people between those dates. That, in my submission, doesn't limit the Prosecution to a joint criminal enterprise which may have had its origins before but which the accused have joined at a later point. It's a matter of when the Trial Chamber finds they joined or had the requisite intention to participate in the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours may not find it was as of September 1991. Your Honours are quite entitled to find the accused joined at different points, at a later point, which is the same point, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Defence of Dr. Simic, while I'm on this issue of responding briefly to several points in his submission, at paragraphs 650 and 651, that's at pages 222 to 223, refers or appears to make an issue of the removal of Bosanski Samac municipality from the Plavsic/Krajisnik indictment. The Prosecution, of course, acknowledges that it no longer forms part of that particular indictment, but notes that Dr. Simic's submissions do not go on to say that the Bosanski Samac municipality is pleaded in three other indictments: Milosevic, the Seselj indictment, and the most recent one in the Tribunal, the Simatovic/Stanisic indictment. I make that submission or that point only in response to the Defence submission in relation to Plavsic. The Prosecution, in its final trial brief, had outlined, at paragraphs 10 and 11 and 12, how the three accused may be guilty of participation in a joint criminal enterprise or acting in concert together in a common design or common purpose to persecute in Bosnia. The Prosecution has said in its brief how the objective requirement is the same for each of the three specific situations which the Tadic Appeals Chamber identified, in which a joint criminal enterprise or common design exists, namely, two or more individuals acting together in the commission of a crime; secondly, a common plan or design or purpose, amounting to or including the commission of one or more crimes in the Statute; and three, the accused's participation in the execution of the common plan, which was related and linked to the commission of one of the crimes provided for in the Statute. The Prosecution says in its oral submissions that in relation to the first one, the evidence discloses that there were numerous participants in this plan or design or enterprise, in both Bosanski Samac municipality and throughout Bosnia, and there had to have been, and the Trial Chamber should have no difficulty in finding, in the Prosecution's submission, that particular aspect is satisfied that there were more than two individuals involved in the commission of the crimes pleaded in the indictment. The Prosecution says in relation to the second one that the Trial Chamber II should have no difficulty in finding beyond a reasonable doubt the existence of the common design, plan, or purpose, amounting to or including the commission of one or more crimes. The Prosecution says the case of that is so overwhelming that the Trial Chamber really only has to turn to whether or not the accused were involved in it, and if so, the degree of their participation. Your Honours, of course, heard from Mr. Zaric, the accused himself, in effect conceding in cross-examination that ethnic cleansing had occurred, that persecution was occurring in Bosnia, was occurring on both sides. The Prosecution also says further, if you look at paragraph 11 of our submissions, in our relation to the mental and its differing requirements according to the three different categories, that is the categories we've outlined in footnote 9, the first category being where all co-defendants acting together pursuant to a common plan possess the same intention. The second one being the so-called camp cases, where the offences charged or alleged have been committed by people acting pursuant to a common plan. And the third being a common design to pursue one course of conduct where one of the perpetrators commits an act where outside of the common design was nevertheless a natural and foreseeable consequence of effecting of the common purpose. The Prosecution says, its submission is, that it can establish or has established in relation -- its evidence in relation to each of those three categories, the accused's requisite intention to participate in either of the three. The accused said the -- the Prosecution says that the joint criminal enterprise or the common plan or design in Bosanski Samac is one which fits into each of the three categories, and the accused's participation can be linked to each of those three particular categories. The Prosecution says that it can establish or has established that, in relation to the first type, the intention being shared by all individuals involved in the commission of the crime, the evidence against Dr. Simic, Mr. Tadic, and Mr. Zaric is such that at the end of the case, the Trial Chamber should be satisfied that each possessed the requisite intention and knowledge of the system of persecutions in Bosanski Samac, shown by their participation in various forms as to render them liable or showing they have the requisite intention under the first category. The second type, the Prosecution says, also fits what happened in Bosanski Samac, that is the accused having knowledge of a system to ill-treat prisoners in relation to the underlying acts of inhumane treatment. The Prosecution says each of the three accused -- the evidence establishes that each of the three accused had the requisite intention or the knowledge of that system and their participation in it in relation to the ill-treatment shows that they shared that participation or shared that intention. The third in the Prosecution's submission is yet another one in which the Prosecution shows the course of the nature of the system, its pervasive extent in Bosanski Samac and the roles, formal and informal of the accused, that they both knew of and intended by their participation, which is shown by their participation to further the common criminal purpose, which was to persecute in Bosnia, specifically in Bosanski Samac. The Prosecution turns to the underlying acts and how they are pleaded in this case. The -- as Your Honours, of course, appreciate, none of the underlying acts of themselves need to be crimes, and of themselves, some of these -- or some of the acts pleaded are not necessarily crimes. However, if committed with the requisite discriminatory intent and when put together, they amount to underlying acts which the Prosecution uses to show discriminatory intention and participation in a system of discrimination or persecutions in Bosanski Samac and elsewhere in Bosnia. The Prosecution's submission is that it does not need to prove the participation of the accused in each and every one of the underlying acts. All it needs to prove is that the -- one of the accused, any one of the accused, -- I'm sorry -- that each of the accused participated in at least one of the underlying acts, and the Prosecution -- and the Trial Chamber is satisfied of that beyond a reasonable doubt. And that particular underlying act is committed with the requisite discriminatory intent to show persecutory -- it's a persecutory crime, and the other elements in relation to a crime against humanity are satisfied, for that accused to be liable for his participation in the criminal enterprise to persecute. The Trial Chamber is entitled to find, if the accused shared the intention or took acts in furtherance, knowingly, of the enterprise, that he is liable for crimes committed by that enterprise as long as they were the natural and foreseeable acts. The Prosecution says that each of the underlying acts pleaded are acts which were committed pursuant to the joint criminal enterprise to persecute, and the participation of any of the accused in any of them show their participation in the joint criminal enterprise of itself. The Prosecution says the difference between the deportation pleaded as an underlying act of the crime against humanity or persecutions -- I withdraw that. I'll rephrase it. The Prosecution says the only difference between participation in deportation as an underlying act of persecutions as a crime against humanity between counts 1 and counts 2 is the intention, the discriminatory intention of the accused. And of course the Prosecution has led the same evidence in relation to the deportation aspect of count 1, count 2 itself, and count 3. The only difference with count 3, of course, being an unlawful transfer -- there's no legal controversy over whether or not the transfer can occur within state or across state borders. But the Prosecution relies upon the evidence in relation to all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On the point of one of the underlying means in count 1, persecutions being (d), deportation, and counts 2 and 3, deportation and transfer, the question that I have is: Why joint criminal enterprise is pleaded only in relation to count 1 and not in relation to counts 2 and 3, where, as we do clearly have the overlap of deportation, expulsion, forcible transfer occurring in essentially all of the counts, albeit there being differences between 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just excuse me for one moment? I can't speak for those who drafted that aspect of the indictment many years ago. All I can say is that the evidence is the same. And in the Prosecution's submission, it doesn't really matter, because whether or not Your Honours are satisfied the deportations occurred pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise to persecute in Bosnia or occurred, as you like, spontaneously or of the volition of the accused in Bosanski Samac doesn't really matter, because Your Honours can isolate the deportation evidence from other parts, if Your Honours were so inclined to find. That is, Your Honours could find that the accused participated individually in deportation, in deporting non-Serbs from Bosanski Samac, without necessarily needing to find they did so as part of a joint criminal enterprise. I'm sorry, Your Honour Judge williams. I just can't answer your question as to why it's pleaded that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It appears to be 10.30, Your Honours. Is that the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break, as usual, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We continue with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As I mentioned before the break, the joint criminal enterprise which the Prosecution has pleaded and of which it has led an abundance of evidence had an ultimate aim to forcibly expel non-Serbs from municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and specifically, in relation to these three accused, in Bosanski Samac. That is, as I outlined at the outset to ethnically cleanse the non-Serbs from the municipality. Your Honours have heard a great deal of evidence about who the participants were in this particular enterprise. The Prosecution's case has been that the enterprise was established at the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and that was set out in Dr. Donia's report, which was the first evidence the Prosecution led in this case, setting out the ambit of the criminal enterprise. The plan to ethnically cleanse or to persecute or to forcibly expel non-Serbs came into operation, the Prosecution says, sometime at least in 1991, and the accused can be shown to have joined by the indictment, sometime during the indictment period, starting from at least the -- starting from, the Prosecution says, about September 1991. The plan involved the highest level coordination between the participants, the participants being the Bosnian Serb leadership; some of the Serb leadership in Belgrade; the Serbian MUP, from where the paramilitaries came; the Yugoslav People's Army, that's the JNA, and its successor, the VRS; the Serbian Democratic Party; and a myriad of individuals who joined and had their own roles within it. Obviously, some people had a much larger and more integral role or an organisational role in the enterprise, whereas others had a smaller role. And this is where Bosanski Samac fits in, because the plan was to ethnically cleanse municipalities in Bosnia, and for it to be implemented, it had to be implemented by willing participants on the ground in each of the municipalities the subject of the plan. Bosanski Samac, as Your Honours have heard, occupying a strategic position between Belgrade and Posavina and the Krajina, the Serbian Krajina, was one of the municipalities in which this particular plan was implemented. The plan, of course, was not done in isolation. It was coordinated. And when I opened and spoke about Bosanski Samac being a textbook example, or a mini-Bosnian example of ethnic cleansing, it shows how all the pieces came -- everything came -- all the pieces came together in this particular municipality. As Your Honours have heard in the evidence, the SDS Main Board issued its instructions or its checklist, that is, the variant A and B instructions in Exhibit P3, containing a checklist or a blueprint for the takeover of municipalities. Variant A, of course, where there was a Serb majority, and Variant B, into which Bosanski Samac fitted, in which there was a non-Serb majority. Your Honours have heard the evidence of how the SDS Main Board issued these instructions, and they were found in various -- or implemented in various other municipalities throughout Bosnia. The Prosecution, of course, acknowledges that it does not have the copy that was sent to Bosanski Samac; however, what happened in Bosanski Samac was so obviously done in accordance with the plan that the only inference, the Prosecution says, available from what happened in Bosanski Samac, in comparison to Variant B of the instructions, is that it was done pursuant to those instructions. The instructions, of course, don't mention Serbian paramilitaries. However, the evidence has been quite clear that the Serbian paramilitaries were brought to Bosanski Samac in advance of the takeover by Todorovic, the Serbian municipality appointed police chief and former co-accused in this case, Milos Bogdanovic, another SDS local apparatchik; and Dr. Simic, as the local SDS president. The evidence quite clearly establishes the three of them colluded in bringing to Bosanski Samac or sending local men to the Serbian Krajina for training and the bringing of them back several days before the takeover of Serbian paramilitaries in camouflage uniforms in anticipation of the takeover. We've put this in our final trial brief and Your Honours have heard the evidence, but they were met, and this is very important. They were brought to Bosanski Samac in JNA helicopters and met by what we call an SDS welcoming committee of prominent SDS members when they arrived. They were housed, they were looked after. And everything the Prosecution says thereafter was in coordination with the local JNA, headed by Colonel Nikolic. In the series of meetings that followed, Dr. Simic made quite clear his position that the Serbian -- that if the non-Serb minorities did not accede to the Serb demands, they would pay for it, and they certainly did. And the evidence quite clearly establishes, in my submission, in the Prosecution's submission, that the Crisis Staff was formed in accordance with and pursuant to the Variant B instructions before the takeover. It was formed on the 15th of April, 1992, two days or the night before, on the eve of the takeover, just as Variant B says a Crisis Staff should be formed. Your Honours have also heard the significant evidence of the arming of the Serb -- sorry - the Serb Territorial Defence and the -- in 1991 and 1992, while at the same time, the JNA was being transformed from a truly national army into a Serb-only army. That too, the Prosecution says the evidence establishes, was in accordance with the greater plan in anticipation of the takeovers which occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina, starting from the end of March 1992. The Prosecution says that the formation of the Serbian municipality too, which is set out in Exhibit P124, was also in accordance with the Variant B instructions, that is, to form a Serbian municipality and to elect the various officials, and the evidence quite clearly establishes that Dr. Simic was elected to a position, Mr. Todorovic was appointed to a position of the police chief, and all the various officials were appointed and elected well before the takeover on the 17th of April, 1992, meaning that everything was put in place beforehand, in anticipation of the takeover, for when the paramilitaries arrived, to spearhead it as the Crisis Staff's shock troops on the ground on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Dr. Simic, in his defence, had to try and find a way around the fact that the evidence of the Samac municipal or Official Gazette, P124, clearly says that the Crisis Staff was established before the takeover. Now, Dr. Simic was aware that he had a difficulty with that, that if it was established and could be shown to have been established before the takeover, the only inference available is that it was done pursuant to Variant B and in anticipation of the takeover, and that the Crisis Staff was involved and pre-informed and knew and went along with the takeover. Dr. Simic's answer to that was to give evidence that - and we say falsely - that it had been actually established after the takeover but just backdated for some sort of administrative convenience. The Prosecution says that explanation is palpably untrue and makes no sense in terms of the evidence, the overwhelming evidence of his knowledge and participation, including, of course, his coincidental presence at Crkvina on the very night of the takeover, in the early hours of the morning, when the paramilitaries were assembling on their way to seize what had been called the vital facilities in the town of Bosanski Samac. Now, against that, of course, is the evidence of the Crisis Staff secretary, Mitar Mitrovic, who the Trial Chamber called proprio motu, him being an important witness to fill in some details missing from the case. One of the most important details that Mitar Mitrovic filled in was who drafted P124, who was responsible for the words saying when the Crisis Staff was established, before the Crisis Staff. And Mitrovic's evidence was that it was Dr. Simic who was responsible for it, who proofread it and corrected it, and Mitar Mitrovic signed it. The evidence, in the Prosecution's submission, is inconvertible. The Crisis Staff was established before the takeover, pursuant to variant B and in anticipation of the forcible takeover on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. The Prosecution also takes Your Honours to the chronology which is annexure A -- annex A to the final trial brief we filed on the 19th of June. And if Your Honours look at the chronology, you can see the convergence of events in both Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bosanski Samac at the same time. Your Honours can see the way we've set it out, is on one side of the page we've got the event in the former Yugoslavia; in the middle we have the date; and on the right-hand side we have the -- what we say is not a coincidental event in Bosanski Samac. The important dates for the implementation in Bosanski Samac and the -- I withdraw that. Your Honours have heard a lot of evidence about the so-called walkout from the Bosnian Serb assembly on the 24th of October, 1991, in relation to the Bosnian parliament or Bosnian assembly's declaration or voting for sovereignty. Your Honours have heard evidence from a constitutional expert, Professor Nikolic, and Dr. Simic especially, his counsel asked many questions of many witnesses in relation to the "vital interests" of the Serbian people and how they were somehow offended by this declaration of sovereignty. In the Prosecution's submission, those details are unnecessary for the determination or the resolution of this case, but for to show how the Bosnian Serb leadership reacted and how it put into place its plan to persecute and ethnically cleanse Bosnian non-Serbs. Your Honours can see from paragraph 36, on the 12th of December, 1991, there was the proclamation of the assembly of the Serbian people, as a federal unit of the federal state of Yugoslavia, which directly followed a resolution passed the day before by the Bosnian Serb parliament -- sorry - the Bosnian parliament, the socialist republic parliament, demanding the JNA defend territories of Bosnia. Your Honours can see that when the EC, that's at paragraph 37, issued guidelines on the recognition of new states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, three days later, the Bosnian Serb -- the SDS leadership responded by issuing or publishing its secret blueprint for the takeovers. That is Variant A and Variant B. Your Honours can see that at paragraph 40, we set out how as soon as Bosnia and Herzegovina - that's on the 20th of December - sought recognition as an independent nation to the Badinter commission, immediately afterwards, Your Honours can see how crisis staffs were established, 43, Bosanska Krupa on the 24th of December, 1991; the 27th of December, Trnovo SDS board meeting. Your Honours can see from the recognition or the Badinter opinions which were published on the 11th of January, 1992, and the recognition of Croatia and Slovenia on the 15th of January. Your Honour can see how the 25th of January the Bosnian Serbs reacted - that's at paragraph 52 - by voting to withdraw from all federal state bodies and organisations. Your Honours can see that when the Bosnian government organised an internationally supervised referendum, that's at paragraph 55, on the 29th of February, 1992, that the Bosnian Serbs reacted by announcing, paragraph 56, a separate Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac. Your Honours can see at that point the Bosnian Serb leadership in Bosanski Samac, headed by Dr. Simic, reacted to the internationally supervised referendum and they reacted according to Variant B by putting it into place, as other municipalities had done so. Your Honours can see that following the referendum - it's in a short history of Bosnia at paragraph 57, the barricades went up in Sarajevo by the Serb paramilitary forces. And Your Honours can see that on the same -- the next day, when the Bosnian government sought international recognition, the Serb -- Bosnian Serbs then proclaimed their own constitution. Your Honours can see that on the 27th of March, 1992, the first takeovers, according to Variant B and Variant A occurred in Bosnia, the first ones in Bosanski Brod and Derventa by paramilitaries in the JNA. It was a pattern which was to emerge or to be followed over the coming months in Bosnia. The very next day, after the first takeover on the 27th of March, the Serbian -- or the Samac Serbian municipality met and elected its officials and appointed Stevan Todorovic as the police chief. Your Honours can see over the page at paragraph 65 and 66, forcible takeovers continued in Bijeljina and Kupres, and that was in the same week that the EC recognised Bosnia as an independent nation and the United States recognised Bosnia. Your Honours can see at paragraph 73 on the 8th of April, there was another takeover, in Foca and Zvornik. It was three days later -- it was at that time - I withdraw that - that very time that Simic, Bogdanovic, and Todorovic sent the local Serb men for training, and it was on the 11th, two weeks later, they returned, in the midst of these early takeovers. Your Honours can see how we've set out -- how one thing followed the other in Bosanski Samac, and that all these things were happening at the same time in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecution says pursuant to the same plan to persecute and using the same modus operandi. The Prosecution says there is absolutely no coincidence here. They were all planned, they were coordinated, as they had to be. And these, of course, took place within the backdrop of the Bosnian Serb leadership's publication of its own six strategic objectives in the Bosnian Serb parliament in May 1992, and in which objective number 1 was: "To establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities." And that, the Prosecution says, is exactly what happened in Bosnia and exactly what happened at the local level in Bosanski Samac. What occurred in Bosanski Samac was part of a widespread and systematic attack or systematic attack on a civilian population. It's widespread because of its scale. It was not just in Bosanski Samac, not just across the municipality, which would of course satisfy the elements or the requirements of that Article 5 charge, but it was also across those municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina where other discriminatory and persecutory attacks were occurring against the non-Serb population. It was also systematic, that is the only conclusion that can be drawn. Systematic, legally, just means that it's organised -- it's systematic because of the organised and improbable nature of its random occurrence. The paramilitaries coming to Bosanski Samac was not random. The SDS bringing them there was not random. The JNA's role in collecting weapons and disarming the population and seizing power or consolidating power before and after the 17th of April was not random. It was organised. It had to have been organised. That's the only inference available from the bulk of evidence as to what occurred in Bosanski Samac which is available. The system which was put in place in Bosanski Samac after the persecutory system, was not a random one. It was not -- it was not spontaneous. It was organised. Upon the takeover, upon the seizure of the main organs of government, of the vital facilities, everything that happened, happened according to a plan. The non-Serbs were rounded up. They were arrested. They were put in facilities. Who controlled the facilities? The facilities were controlled by the Crisis Staff, which was the acting in place of the municipality which had taken over the municipality from the democratically elected government. The TO was the Crisis Staff. The SUPs, the MUPs. The schools were the crisis staffs. The police were acting in coordination with the Crisis Staff and the JNA, and then the VRS. All of the participants were acting together. They had to have been. There is no other way that persecution on this scale could have been organised and carried out over that period. The looting and plunder was organised. It was organised through the Crisis Staff, through its civil protection. The use of labourers, as Mr. Weiner, Mr. Di Fazio, will address you in greater detail later, was organised. It had to have been organised. The Prosecution submits that, as we've set out at paragraph 92 of our final trial brief, in referring to the Kvocka trial judgement, summarising persecutions, that many of the things referred to in the Kvocka judgement, where it has summarised findings of persecution in the Tribunal, are present in Bosanski Samac. The Kvocka trial chamber found thus far the Trial Chambers of the ICTY have found the following acts may constitute persecution when committed with the requisite discriminatory intent. I'll read you the relevant ones: Imprisonment; unlawful detention of civilians or infringement upon individual freedom; murder; deportation or forcible transfer; seizure, collection, segregation and forced transfer of civilians to camps; plunder of property; attacks upon towns - sorry - cities, towns, and villages; trench-digging; and denying of bank account, educational, or employment opportunities on the basis of religion. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber in Kvocka's statement, set out just before paragraph 93, that "the Trial Chamber reads this statement as meaning that jointly or severally, the acts alleged in the amended indictment must amount to persecution, not that each discriminatory act alleged must be individually regarded as a violation of international law." The Prosecution submits that is a correct statement of the law, and this Trial Chamber should follow the Kvocka trial chamber's finding in that regard. In relation to the forcible takeover, which is about the fifth bullet point in the outline - I've gone into some of it - I wish to take Your Honours to the differing defences which the three accused appear to have run during this trial. Dr. Simic's defence on the whole appears to be that it was the paramilitaries who took over the town, the municipality, and that the formation of the Crisis Staff was a spontaneous reaction of concerned Serb citizens to fill the vacuum of power. Mr. Tadic appears to be saying that it was the paramilitaries and not the JNA, and Mr. Simic - I'm sorry - Mr. Zaric appears to be saying that it was the paramilitaries and the Crisis Staff acting together. The Prosecution says that all three are true. It was the Crisis Staff, it was the JNA, it was the paramilitaries, and that they were all acting together, in concert, pursuant to the plan. In fact, the document P127, which is the 13 signatory reports, is really in the category that the Prosecution says of a public confession of a forcible persecutory takeover, and it too appears to mirror all the requirements or instructions under Variant B and Variant A as to how to go about taking over a municipality. The first part refers to -- the first paragraph, the organised arming of the Serbian people in particular. The second part refers to the arrival of the paramilitaries and the way that the local JNA commander referred to them as a "legal elite of Serbian commandos" and explained that he was putting them under his control before the takeover. It then goes on to talk about -- this is a document which of course Mr. Zaric was one of the authors of, in fact, was the author of author of, the person who drafted it for the signature of the other 12, by talking about this group played an indisputably positive role in the "liberation" of Samac as part of the special battalion and in fighting in other places. It then referred to its negative role, that is, they went a little bit too far in looting, banditry, all times of crimes. And their official role, as printed, as war criminals in the area. It also refers to the role of the Crisis Staff and the removal of the -- in the removal of the leader of the 4th Detachment-- 2nd Posavina Brigade and then fourth, saying when the war broke out, that's on page 2, first the Crisis Staff and then the War Presidency of Samac came under the influence of a handful of individuals, led by Crni, that's the paramilitary psychopath about whom the Trial Chamber has heard an abundance of evidence, and privatising their positions in the civilian government. And fifth, with the blessing of those who had brought them in, that's the Crisis Staff, and those who had sent them, they engaged in unheard of looting of privately and socially owned property transferred to Serbia. The document, the public confession of the discriminatory nature of this takeover continues: "The massive arrests and isolation of Croat and Muslims followed without any criteria, and some of the prisoners were subjected to measures such as abuse, torture, or even killing, characteristic only of war criminals of Ustasha origin." And then refers to the Crkvina massacre committed by Lugar and the paramilitaries. I mean, that document contemporaneously, and more eloquently sets out more than the Prosecution can hope exactly what occurred in Bosanski Samac in 1992 and exactly what people knew about what was happening in Bosanski Samac in 1992. In relation to the discriminatory nature of the takeover, the Trial Chamber, of course, heard even Defence witnesses agreed with the Prosecution case. A notable one was Mr. Radovan Antic's successor as head of the 4th Detachment, that's the local JNA, Mr. Jovo Savic, who agreed that a takeover by one ethnicity at the expense of others, as described in the 13 signatories, that's at page 17.167, would cause interethnic conflict. But more importantly, he agreed that the paramilitary formations, that's the paramilitaries, the Serbian paramilitaries, led by Crni, Lugar, and Debeli, and brought to Bosanski Samac from -- under the control of Frenki Simatovic in Belgrade, had in fact "entered the municipality in order to carry out an organised campaign of terror against the innocent population." That's non-Serbs. He agreed with that proposition, at page 1713. He also agreed -- this is -- and I stress this: The leader of the 4th Detachment, several days after the takeover -- after he replaced Antic, agreed with this proposition. What that means is that the takeover which you saw by Serb forces over territory in which the Serbs were not a majority was a forcible takeover on discriminatory or ethnic grounds, wasn't it? And Mr. Savic's answer was yes. He also agreed that the effect of the JNA non-action was to allow the -- that's on the 17th of April, 1992, in not restoring the elected -- democratically elected government to power, was to allow the paramilitaries and the civilian authorities to seize control on an ethnic basis. That's at page 17191. An ethnic basis, that is, a discriminatory basis. And it allowed the paramilitaries and the Serb police to install a Serb government, a Serb-only government, over a municipality with a non-Serb majority. He agreed with that. But importantly, for the intention and proof of the intention and knowledge of the accused, in particular for Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zaric, Mr. Savic, their commanding officer, said, agreed: Everyone in the 4th Detachment command, that's them, was aware that the effect of the JNA's inaction was that an ethnic-based takeover was allowed to occur in Bosanski Samac, page 17191. Yes, he said. Repeated, everyone in the command, and you've said that people disagreed with what happened, that is you, Antic, Tadic, Zaric, everyone else in the command was aware at the time, that's April 1992, that the effect of the JNA's inaction was to allow the installation of a new regime on discriminatory ethnic grounds. That was the question. Mr. Jovo Savic, the commander of the JNA 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac answer was: We knew that. It goes on. Question: The capture of territory in the Bosanski Samac municipality by the paramilitaries and others could not have been a positive liberation for the non-Serb majority that was living there, was it? His answer, quite candidly, we say: "I will say no." It's page 17193. And when asked about the 13 signatories, P127, and the use of the word "liberation," the question was: From what you've just said and the questions and answers in the last few minutes, what you really mean, what that really means, doesn't it, is that this group, that's the paramilitaries, played an indisputably positive role in the military takeover on ethnic grounds in Bosanski Samac and the installation of a Serb-only government. That's really what it means, isn't it?" To which Mr. Jovo Savic at 17.195 of the transcript replied: "Yes." Of course, the Defence called its own constitutional expert, Professor Nikolic, who in cross-examination of the -- in relation to the wonderful set of human rights guarantees which are part of Republika Srpska constitution, agreed that those very actions, that is, the takeover of a municipality by one ethnicity, forcing out the others, would have been contrary to the Republika Srpska constitution. And he said: "Any discrimination on national grounds is absolutely unacceptable." That's at pages 12.168 to 170 of the transcript. I also want to refer Your Honours to an aspect of the proceedings explored in a little bit of detail and that's the Crkvina massacre. In the Prosecution's submission, that does have some importance in relation to the role of the JNA and the coordination between the paramilitaries, JNA, Crisis Staff, and other participants in the enterprise or the takeover of Bosanski Samac. And the significance is this: Your Honours have heard evidence, the Prosecution says cogent evidence, of the date, being the 7th of May, 1992. Mr. Zaric in his own book, which is P180, at page 185, himself says -- and Your Honours have heard a lot of evidence from Mr. Zaric that he took a lot of contemporaneous notes including, one must assume, of this particular event and took them at the time. In his book he said: "A monstrous event happened on the afternoon of 7th of May, 1992." Prosecution says that's the best evidence from Mr. Zaric as to the date of that. Now, it's important because Zaric in his record of interview or his statement to the Prosecutor says that Nikolic and P127 says that Nikolic took the paramilitaries under his control before the takeover. P174 and 175 are the orders signed by Nikolic on the 7th of May subordinating those same psychopathic paramilitary thugs to his command to clear two particular roads in two particular operations. The Prosecution says the only interference available from Nikolic's prevarication as to the date and his contention that once he found out about the massacre, he withdrew the subordination orders, and of course no evidence is before the Trial Chamber of that, whereas the Prosecution has produced evidence of the subordination. Prosecution says the only inference available is that Nikolic has given his evidence of that in return for Zaric shifting his story as to the date, and when he informed Nikolic. Because if Nikolic was informed on the day and those paramilitaries were under his command after he was informed, he had a responsibility to punish them for this atrocity, and that is why, in my submission, the Prosecution's submission, Nikolic backed away and prevaricated as to when he found out and came up with this story we say, as to his withdrawal of subordination. The Prosecution says this is important in the whole scheme because it shows how the two groups, paramilitaries and JNA, were acting together before and after the takeover. The Prosecution, turning to the final aspect of point 2, which is the joint criminal enterprise and the role of the three accused. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber should have no difficulty at all in finding that Mr. -- sorry -- Dr. Simic knew, participated, and committed acts in furtherance of the enterprise to persecute in Bosanski Samac. The Prosecution said his role was integral. He was at the apex of the system. And we emphasise the word "system," because that's what it was, of persecutions implemented and directed against the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac. Apart from the things I've already outlined, I take Your Honours to the meeting held in response to the 2nd Posavina Brigade's publication of P127, the 13 signatories report. The meeting held in early December 1992, which Crisis Staff members attended. Your Honours heard evidence from various participants, Mr. Zaric, Mr. Tubakovic, Mr. Erletic. I ask Your Honours to accept the candid evidence of Mr. Tubakovic and Mr. Erletic as to what happened at that meeting, which goes directly to Dr. Simic's contemporaneous knowledge. If he denies it, and he's denied it loudly, his knowledge of anything that was happening, of exactly what the allegations were, and many of the allegations in that document are similar to those in the indictment the three accused face. Simic -- what was Simic's response? His response, according to the witnesses, was to attack -- was not to deny the truth of the allegations but to express his annoyance that they had been made. That goes to both his participation and to his knowledge. Right bang in the middle of the indictment period, Your Honours. In relation to Mr. Tadic, the Prosecution too says you should have no difficulty in finding his participation in the enterprise from at least before the takeover right through to the end of the indictment period, because of his role on the crisis -- in the takeover, on the Crisis Staff, and as the Crisis Staff's chief negotiator in the exchanges. Tadic participated fully in Crisis Staff decision-making, in those vital early days when they seized power and put their persecutory system into place, in those vital early days when they implemented it, when the plan was -- in those -- I withdraw that. The only inference available from his participation and his continued participation right throughout the indictment period is of not just his knowledge but of his intention to further it. One cannot participate in a system of deportations, taking people, tortured people, from imprisonment, putting them on buses and deporting them to another country without knowledge of what was going on and sharing that knowledge. You could not do it and you could not do not do it for that length of time without sharing the intention. The Prosecution says you can find from Mr. Savic's evidence in particular that everyone on the command, including Tadic, knew of the discriminatory nature of the takeover when it occurred. Turning to Zaric. Now, Mr. Zaric, and he tried to back away from this, was appointed from the Crisis Staff in those vital early days, we say, as the chief of national security. It was while he was the chief of national security that he was entering the Crisis Staff and MUP-controlled prisons where prisoners were being treated in the most abominable and was able to interrogate the most important political prisoners. It was Zaric who was entrusted with that most sensitive and delicate of tasks. It was Zaric they entrusted with the job of interviewing - I'm sorry - of going on TV with political prisoners and using them as tools of the Serb authorities. It was Zaric who was able to remove the severely mistreated prisoners from one form of detention, that's allegedly "civilian" to military. None of these people were, of course, POWs. It was Zaric who managed to remove them from one form of custody, where they were inhumanely treated, to another, where they were also inhumanely treated, although not as badly as before. It was Mr. Zaric who told some of these prisoners that they were political prisoners, and it was Zaric who, in his own words in his own book, said he moved them from one place to another to continue the interrogations. It was also Zaric, as Your Honours saw on the tape of the propaganda exercise, P16A, the transcript shows Zaric saying: "However, I must say that the special units of the Territorial Defence and the Serbian police did a good job. Time will show this was for the good of the people," in reference to the takeover. The Prosecution says that Mr. Zaric's own words and those of his own witnesses prove his knowledge, his mens rea, his intention. His own -- Mr. Zaric was considered important enough in the scheme of persecutions in Bosanski Samac, conducted by the military and the civilians, the SDS, to be provided with his own driver, Mr. Tutnjevic. Mr. Tutnjevic provided interesting evidence, from the Prosecution's viewpoint, because he agreed with the Prosecution that both he and Mr. Zaric at the time knew of the isolation of the non-Serbs, their unlawful arrest, the actions of the volunteers and the mistreatment of non-Serb prisoners by the police. That's at page 17503. But it goes further. Mr. Zaric's long-term friend, retired senior police investigator Vladimir Sarkanovic - who was working in the police station interrogating up to a hundred of these people, these non-Serbs who had been imprisoned on persecutory grounds - talked about the system. He was asked -- we asked him in cross-examination, at page 16592: This system which allowed the establishment of these centres which housed hundreds of non-Serbs also allowed Muslim women, children, and Croat women to be rounded up and detained at various times. His answer: Yes, he was aware of it. Then, and this is very important in relation to Mr. Zaric's knowledge of what was happening in the police station, the condition of the prisoners, and the system of persecutions. Question: "Everyone working in the police station, that's the SUP in Bosanski Samac, in April and May and June 1992, was aware of this system of arrest, detention, and mistreatment of non-Serb prisoners, weren't they?" Answer: "More or less, everyone. Some of them had even been involved in that." It goes on, at 16599. I'm asking you about the system in place. You've agreed that there was a system in place in Bosanski Samac. He said I've already said that. He agrees twice with the proposition there was this persecutory system in place at the police station. Now, when the Prosecution asked Mr. Zaric about Mr. Sarkanovic's evidence along these lines at page 20046. Yes. "Now, your friend Mr. Sarkanovic has said in this court that there was a system of persecution being developed against the non-Serbs and that everyone working from the police station was aware of it. You too were aware of the system of persecution, weren't you?" Answer: "I was not working for the police station, but I was aware of that fact." Yet knowing that, knowing that he was aware of the fact that the system of persecution in place against the people in detention, Zaric willingly participated in their further humiliation, including forcing them to sign coerced statements. Mr. Savic also agreed with the proposition from the Prosecution about the system of arrests. Again, that's the commanding officer of the 4th Detachment. At page 17166, question: "From what you had seen, those people were pursuing, that is, the non-Serb authorities, were pursuing policies against the non-Serbs that could only be described as discriminatory, that is, arresting them, detaining them, torturing them, because they were non-Serbs?" Answer: "Yes." And it goes on. "And that discrimination which you saw and heard about in Bosanski Samac after the 17th of April, by the people you criticised in P127, the 13 signatories, could really only be described as persecutions against those non-Serbs in that period, couldn't it?" To which the then commander of the JNA replied: "Yes, you could see -- you could say that." Mr. Zaric's own words in cross-examination also showed his knowledge of the system of persecutions before he removed the prisoners from the TO to Brcko on the 26th of April. And that's at page 19988 of the transcript, in cross-examination. Now -- question: "Now, of course you were aware of that, but by the very fact of your intervention by taking prisoners to Brcko on the 26th of April, you were aware of the emergence of the consequences of discriminatory behaviour as of the 26th of April, weren't you? That was the question." Answer: "The 26th of April? You mean when those people went to Brcko."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I was convinced that the non-Serb population of the municipality was being treated improperly. Over the page, 19990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware of this discrimination on ethnic grounds that's the prisoners in custody as of the 26th of April, weren't you, based on a number of things, the singing of Chetnik songs, the ethnicity of the people in custody, the cursing of their balija mothers and so on, and the insults directed towards them by their captors. All of those things convinced you, as of the 26th of April, 1992, that these prisoners were being discriminated against on ethnic grounds, didn't they?" And this is very important for the Trial Chamber's deliberation in terms of Mr. Zaric's contemporaneous knowledge. His answer was: "Not only the 26th. I saw such scenes from the outset. I think that such things happened even before, and I agree. In my view, the measures that were taken were improper, they were discriminatory, and they deserve condemnation." That, in the Prosecution's submission, makes complete Mr. Zaric's knowledge of the system of persecutions before the 26th of April, when he says he moved people from custody because of what was happening there. The Prosecution says -- submits that when you put all those things together, the only rationale conclusion that the Trial Chamber can draw is that Mr. Zaric participated knowingly and willingly and in furtherance of the persecution from at least, at least, the date of the takeover, although the Prosecution says you can infer his knowledge of the fact that there was to be a persecutory takeover from events before, such as his role, his crucial role in military intelligence, his network of informers, the system he had in place, and what he says in his book, P180, at page 141, when he refers to a conversation with Mr. Nikolic before the takeover, in relation to Mr. Izet Izetbegovic, where he says: "I dared not ask him too directly what we could expect here or even more directly how the Serb question would be resolved in Posavina, but approached the subject in a roundabout way. I said, Haven't Zvornik, Bijeljina, and Vlasenica been a lesson to Izetbegovic not to oppose the Serbs and which municipality is next?" That's page 141 of his own book, written after he was indicted, showing that he knew well in advance that the Serbs were forcibly taking over towns and municipalities in Bosanski Samac, and this is at the time when the paramilitaries had arrived in Bosanski Samac, just as they had in those other municipalities referred to. I turn to -- and I'll do this fairly briefly - point number 3. The heading is: "Response to Legal Issues Raised in Simic's Final Trial Brief." There's two issues. One, international armed conflict, and the second is the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina and self-determination. The Defence of Dr. Simic has made some submissions in relation to findings of an international armed conflict. Your Honours have ruled part way through the trial that you would make this decision based upon the evidence before you. The Trial Chamber of course has heard an abundance of evidence as to the fact that there was an armed conflict, an international one, between Croatia and the Republic of -- the former - sorry - the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on the border, at the time. Your Honours have also heard an enormous amount of evidence of shelling from Croatia and attacks by the HVO and the HV, that's the Croatian army, in tandem. The only inference or -- the Prosecution goes further. It says that it is so overwhelming that there is no other inference available but that there was an international armed conflict occurring at the time. That of course is relevant to the third count, the Article 2, grave breaches count. In addition to our submissions in the final trial brief, the Prosecution refers you to two other cases, that is, the Tadic Appeals Chamber judgement of the 15th of July, 1999, at paragraph 147. That's in relation to the overall control test of the VRS and the JNA. And the Appeals Chamber held: "It now falls to the Appeals Chamber to establish whether, in the circumstances of the case, the Yugoslav army exercised, in 1992, the requisite measure of control over the Bosnian Serb army. The answer must be in the affirmative." The Appeals Chamber developed this - between paragraphs 146 and 162 - and decided that the conflict between the Bosnian Serbs and the central authorities, that's the Bosnian government, was international even after the 9th of May, 1992, which was the date of formal withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also refer you to the Celebici Appeals Chamber judgement of the 20th of February, 2001, where the Appeals Chamber there confirmed the Trial Chamber's decision that the armed conflict taking place in Bosnia after the 19th of May, 1992, could be regarded as international. That's at paragraph 50. Two further cases in relation to the HVO being under the effective control of the HV. That's the Prosecution and Blaskic, trial judgement of 3rd of March, 2000, and Prosecution versus Kordic and Cerkez of the 26th of February, 2001. The Prosecution simply says that in the light of the overwhelming amount of evidence already heard by this Trial Chamber, we invite you, if necessary, to take judicial notice of the findings of these other cases as to the -- especially the Appeals Chambers as to the nature of the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant time. The Prosecutor says these are not matters which require any further litigating. They have been well established. The final submission is in relation to the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina and self-determination. Dr. Simic has made a number of arguments about the constitutional status of Bosnia at the time the walkout from the Serb -- sorry - the Bosnian legislature and the fact that they say that Bosnia could not have been regarded as a state during the indictment period until Dayton. The Prosecution's response to this is that the logical outcome of what they're saying -- I withdraw that. I'm sorry. Is that Your Honours need only consider the date of admission to the United Nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Slovenia on the 22nd of May, 1992, and the declaration or the secession of Serbia and Montenegro on the 27th of April, 1992. The logical outcome of their argument is that none of the Yugoslav republics were nations at the relevant time. The Prosecution asks -- says that the Trial Chamber should disregard these arguments in their entirety. They are to use the English vernacular, a complete red herring. They are irrelevant to the Trial Chamber's determination as to whether or not serious violations of international humanitarian law occurred on the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1992 and 1993. They also raised the issue of the status -- of self-determination in the context of the Bosnian Serb people and their establishment of the Republika Srpska. The Prosecution repeats its submission that these arguments are irrelevant. They should have no bearing on the Trial Chamber's determination of whether violations of international humanitarian law were committed. But we refer you, if Your Honours need further elucidation on this point, to the articles of James Crawford and Lawrence Eastwood, particularly Eastwood, his summary at page 301 of the article we filed, and of Professor Crawford's at page 113 of the article we filed. Those are my submissions. I'll leave the next part to Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, Mr. Re has outlined to you the position of the Prosecution in respect of the joint criminal enterprise and the role played by the defendants in that. I wish to address you on the system of exchanges which was in effect in the Prosecution case nothing more than forcible transfer or deportation and is pleaded as an underlying act in the first count of persecutions. Referring to the plan to ethnically cleanse, the Prosecution said in its final trial brief that the plan was designed -- "designed to make life so unbearable that the non-Serbs left, thinking they had no choice or involuntarily applied to leave the new Serb territories, or alternatively, the Serb authorities simply deported the non-Serbs to another territory." Prosecution brief, paragraph 19. The mechanism by which this was achieved was the system of exchanges. The system of exchanges, if Your Honours please, was a complex series of arrangements requiring many actors and people coming in at different times, different pieces of equipment were required to facilitate it and bring it about. You required negotiators, you required guards, you required radio sets in the communications room to communicate with, in the main, the Croatian side. You required cooperation with the military to ensure that prisoners who were being held in JNA prisons were included in the numbers of people being expelled from the territory of Bosanski Samac. You required the Red Cross to prepare the lists, by going into the prisons and asking the beaten and tortured men who were being held there the hollow question: Do you want to leave via an exchange? It required all of these actors and all of these facilities and all of these arrangements. It required administrative bodies to be set up, the Exchange Commissions, to oversee the processes. And each of these three defendants played a crucial and important role in some aspect of those deportations, through this system of exchanges. The Prosecution case is that in fact the word "exchange" is really nothing more than a sinister euphemism for the deportation and forcible transfer of the people, the non-Serbs of Bosanski Samac. The Prosecution case is that when people were exchanged through this system that I've described, they were being in fact deported or transferred involuntarily. The Defence case, on the other hand, is that, at least insofar as Blagoje Simic and Miroslav Tadic are concerned, is that persons who were exchanged left voluntarily. Their position is that the system, far from being a cruel system of deportation and forcible transfer, was in fact a humanitarian exercise. This was the work of humanists. And you heard that expression often throughout the evidence given by the Defence witnesses. Mr. Tadic said in his brief that the decision on whether someone wished to leave the municipality was "exclusively taken by the individual who freely disposed of that right, without use of any force, threatening, and coercion, by Miroslav Tadic or third parties." You'll find that at paragraph 353 of his brief. Mr. Simic makes clear in his final trial brief that the exchanges were voluntarily in nature and asserts that "many of the non-Serbs voluntarily returned from the exchange line to Samac, which is a unique phenomenon in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina." Paragraph 205 of his brief. At paragraph 348 and 349 of his brief, Dr. Simic had this to say: "It was the decision of each individual whether to remain or stay. If they decided to stay, the refusal was passed on to the ICRC, who would inform the requesting person of the refusal. If the requested person or persons decided to leave, they were allowed to pack and to go, and the exchange line located -- to go, and the exchange line -- to the exchange line located on the border between Republika Srpska and the state of Croatia. "Many people chose to remain. In fact, so many chose to remain that eventually the ICRC insisted that the family member or members being sought had to be brought to the exchange line in order to ensure that the decisions to remain in Bosanski Samac were voluntarily. The fact that so many chose to stay confirms and corroborates the fact that the decision to leave was voluntary. The fact that many others returned back from the exchange line is further confirmation that their decision to either leave or stay was voluntary and that no one felt coerced into leaving." Just pausing there, there is not one jot of evidence in the case to support the proposition that the ICRC insisted that the family member or members had to be brought to the exchange line in order to ensure that the decision to remain in Bosanski Samac was voluntary. If anything, there is the evidence of Mr. Tadic's witnesses, in particular, Mr. Velimir Maslic, that it was the Croats who insisted that such persons be taken to the exchange point, and it was the Croats who needed reassuring that in fact the person did not wish to cross.
