Two major planks of the Defence case, if Your Honours please, to show and illustrate the voluntariness of the -- the supposed voluntariness of the exchange, of the exchange system, was the system of so-called family reunification; and secondly, this matter I've already alluded to, the voluntary nature of the exchange being -- exchanges being illustrated by the numbers of people who returned, and the endorsements on the exchange lists that you see from time to time, such as returned or did not cross. Those two issues form a large part of the Defence submission. So the battle lines are clearly drawn in this case. Voluntariness lies at the heart of the issue concerning exchanges and deportation. That is the point at which the Defence and the Prosecution case collide directly. No party to these proceedings denies the existence of the system of exchanges. No party to these proceedings denies that it was -- the number of people leaving via the exchanges from Bosanski Samac were overwhelmingly non-Serb, and no party denies that the numbers of people entering Bosanski Samac were overwhelmingly Serb, numbers of people entering through the system of exchanges. Before I turn to the issue of voluntariness in more detail, I wish to briefly address you on the issue of the law. Mr. Re has already gone into this in some -- touched upon it. If Your Honours please, the charges of persecution, deportation, and unlawful deportation in the three counts all involve notions of deportation and forcible transfer. There is a controversy, and we point this out at paragraph 99 -- would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, there is some controversy as to the nature of forcible transfer and deportation, and we have alerted you to that in paragraph 99 of our closing brief, namely, the issue of whether or not deportation requires a transfer across a national boundary or whether it can include forcible transfer within a country. That more restrictive definition of deportation has been adopted in Krstic and Krnojelac; in Krstic at paragraph 521, the Krstic Trial Chamber decision; and in Krnojelac at paragraph 474. And in this particular case, of course, most of the forcible movement of people involves deportation to Croatia across national boundaries. You will also see from annex A that there is also evidence of forcible transfer within Bosnia and that a number of witnesses spoke of their forcible transfer within Bosnia, namely, to Sarajevo, two witnesses in particular who spring to mind are Witness L and Mr. Izet Izetbegovic. But deportation across national boundaries is by far the main method that was used to expel people from their homes and the territory of Bosanski Samac in this particular case, and that's sufficient for all three charges. I want to briefly quote to you from Krnojelac on the notion of voluntariness, because that's the issue that I'm particularly interested in. In Krnojelac, the Trial Chamber had this to say on the issue of voluntariness, at paragraph 47(v) page 199 of the decision: "Deportation is illegal only where it is forced. Forced is not to be interpreted in a restrictive manner, such as being limited to physical force. It may include the threat of force or coercion, such as that caused by fear of violence, duress, detention, psychological oppression, or abuse of power against such person or persons or another person or by taking advantage of a coercive environment. The essential element is that the displacement be involuntary in nature, where the relevant persons had no real choice. Forced displacement is only illegal where it occurs without grounds permitted by international law." That, in the Prosecution submission, makes clear that there is to be a realistic and sensible approach to the nature of choice and voluntariness of movement of peoples, and the Prosecution adopts that and submits that it provides useful guidance to you when you come to assess the notion of voluntariness as applied to the people who left via the system of exchanges. There were a number of categories of persons who left via the system of exchanges, categories of persons revealed by the evidence. Firstly, there were the prisoners who were being held in the detention centres or torture chambers as they should be more aptly described as. Those who were approached in those places and asked if they wished to be exchanged. One such witness was Mr. Dragan Lukac. He testified to you of the beatings and torture that he had endured at the hands of his captors and he testified to you of the various movements that he was subjected to, being taken from prison to prison in and out of Bosnia. And you will find that testimony at 1791 of the transcript. He said that he was in his cell in the SUP building on the night of the 3rd of September, when Mr. Svetozar Vasovic, a man who had a high role -- a prominent role in the exchanges, approached him and his cellmate, Franjo Barukcic, another man who had endured almost unimaginable torture and beatings, and asked them if they wanted to be exchanged. And he said: "Of course, we said we did." The Prosecution invites you to place yourself in the position of Mr. Dragan Lukac, not only in relation to him but because his position was so similar to many other prisoners who found themselves in those places, and ask yourselves if he had the slightest choice in relation to his answer. If there was anything he could say but "yes, I want to be exchanged." The Prosecution's submission is that a moment's reflection on the evidence that's been presented before you will compel you, must compel you, to conclude that he had absolutely no choice whatsoever. The choice was between continued and further beatings and torture, watching his comrades being beaten and tortured. The choice was between the possibility of some psychopath like Lugar or one of the other paramilitaries suddenly wandering in one day and shooting them and killing them, as had happened so often in those prisons and detention centres in Bosanski Samac. That was his choice. The Prosecution's submission is that, clearly, the question that was asked of him - Do you want to be exchanged? - was nothing but a hollow, cruel sham, and a question that had no real meaning or significance at all in any sense of the word. So from that point of view, there was absolutely no voluntariness involved in his particular exchange. The only choice he had was survival and possible freedom from the extended torture and beating that he was suffering. Sometimes that fraudulent and sham question was not asked at all. Sometimes the niceties weren't even observed at all. That might be another category of person that we could create. There were a number of them. I've chosen to mention just one of them, one of the witnesses who was simply taken out of his torture cell and taken to the exchange point, and that is the witness Mr. Dragan Delic. He testified to you of undergoing a truly shocking period of torture and beatings. He testified to you of witnessing unrestrained orgies of violence in the primary school, he testified to you of having his teeth pulled out with pliers, he testified to you of seeing all sorts of unbelievable acts of sexual violence in his holding cell. And he was exchanged on the morning of the 4th of September. He didn't even know until he was taken to be exchanged that he was going to be exchanged. This is what he had to say on this particular issue:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of the 4th of September, did you know you were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the morning of the 4th of September, a policeman came and called out my name. He told me to follow him. We walked to the SUP building. In the hallway of that building, he told me to stop and wait for him there. I waited for half an hour while he went off somewhere. And then he came back and he told me to follow him again. We got into a car and when we were inside the car he told me: You're going to be exchanged now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until that point, had you had any idea that that was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was afraid they were taking me again for interrogation at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but had you had any idea up until that time that that was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had anyone consulted with you as to whether or not you wished to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No one spoke to him, no one consulted with him. He was just taken to the exchange point and kicked out of the town in which he had lived all his life. And there were a number of other witnesses who are in exactly the same position. No questions asked, someone would come and take them out of their prison, put them on a bus, the bus which had been organised by Mr. Tadic, and they would be taken to the deportation point and kicked out of their municipality and their town. If Your Honours please, it's -- do you wish me -- I've reached a natural break in my submission. Do you want to take the break now or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless you're starting a new section, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to deal with this, but I'd prefer if I could deal with the next session in one portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We shall take our break now and continue at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, if you want a Defence perspective on this issue of voluntariness of the exchange system, you don't have to do any better than to go to the evidence of Mr. Tubakovic. He was asked this question, and provided this answer:.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that a lot of people didn't leave voluntarily. The document you signed, referring to the 13 signatories document, Exhibit P127, talks about the arrests of people, the isolation of people, and people who were locked up and exchanged, and that process meant they weren't leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I agree that these measures were taken and that these people were mistreated, isolated, arrested, detained, and locked up, and so on. And this increased their wish to leave, and of course under pressure and wishing to escape from these misfortunes, they left. That is logical. I can't provide -- sorry - you'll find that evidence at pages 19355. Now, that's an insight for a man who was there on the ground at the time, a man who would be prepared to see things from a Serb perspective and yet that is still his evidence. That is a powerful and compelling piece of testimony to illustrate to you just how involuntary these movements of people through the exchange system was. But in the Prosecution's submission, you should, with respect, you shouldn't really be troubled too much by the plight of the prisoners who were held in detention. The conditions they suffered were so horrific, so relentlessly horrific, that it really cannot possibly be a question of choice as to their departure via the system of exchanges. You may, however, be a little more exercised of this inquiry when you come to consider the civilians who were living in Bosanski Samac. You heard a lot of testimony from the Prosecution witnesses of the conditions that they lived under from April of 1992 up until their time of departure. The Prosecution wants to ask you, request, that you consider the situation of the civilians by stepping into the shoes of one of those people, one of the witnesses who came along and testified to you of their life in the months following April 17, 1992. Snjezana Delic was one such person, and she provides, in the Prosecution submission, a good example to look at, precisely because of the normality of her existence prior to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, and because of the abnormality of her existence following that date. Up until April of 1992, she had lived a normal existence in Bosanski Samac. She went to school in Bosanski Samac. She met and married her husband in Bosanski Samac. And after studying in Sarajevo, she took up a position at the high school as the economics teacher. Her two children were born in Bosanski Samac in 1981 and 1984. Her husband, Dragan Delic, was born in Doboj, a nearby town, and he also went to school in Bosanski Samac, and he worked as the president of the managing board of the Mebos company. So that was a family whose entire existence and life was centred around the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Consider, then, how she saw events unfold before her eyes after the 17th of April, 1992. The first thing that she would have witnessed, become aware of, was the destruction of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. The municipality of Bosanski Samac had hitherto, up until that point, represented the three ethnic groups. In one night it was gone and a new municipality had replaced it, the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac. The body that had represented her ethnic group had ceased to exist. She was a Croat, of course. That's the first thing that she would have seen. Five days later, on the 22nd -- sorry, not five days later. A month later, on the 22nd of May, her husband was arrested. By that stage, she would have seen the wave of arrests of non-Serbs that was already occurring in Bosanski Samac. She said, page 6397: "He went to the police station, and after about an hour or two, he called on the telephone, and only said: I have this opportunity. I have been permitted to call you. And I'll be staying here for a while. After that, he did not come home." That was another event that was unfolding in front of Mrs. Delic. She would have seen the signs being posted around the towns on the chestnut trees, nailed to the chestnut trees, prohibiting the gathering of three or more non-Serbs. She thinks this occurred in June, but the preponderance of the evidence in the case says it occurred much earlier than that. You can imagine how she as a Croat would have felt, being unable to associate and gather in large groups with members of her own ethnic group. On the 7th of May, or very soon thereafter, she would have become aware of the Crkvina massacre, in which a large number of Croatian prisoners who had been held were summarily slaughtered in a small factory by Lugar and the other madmen whom he associated with. Can you imagine how she would have felt, knowing that that had happened, and sometime later her husband being summarily arrested by Mr. Todorovic and placed in a prison? She would have known that absolutely nothing was done by the new authorities in town about that particular matter. It's another event that would have unfolded before her eyes. In May, the police came around to her house looking for her Ustasha brother. Can you imagine how Mrs. Delic would have felt being visited by the police, knowing what was going on in the town? In mid-May of 1992, Mrs. Delic was warned by a kindly neighbour of the round-up of Croats that was going on, being put on trucks and taken to Zasavica. She had to flee with her children to another apartment to avoid being caught in the round-up. That's the first round-up that she avoided successfully. Can you imagine how Mrs. Delic would have felt by that stage? She had been left without a job. She didn't have a job. Her husband was in jail. When she tried to get money out of the bank, she couldn't do that. She was cut off from money. She had no source of funds. You'll find that evidence at 6399. Now she didn't have money. What was she to do? On the 27th of June, Stojan Blagojevic came around and took her car, the family car, gave her a scrap of paper, that's P49, authorising its seizure, its confiscation, in the name of the Crisis Staff. She didn't have a car any more. What property was going to go next, she might have wondered. You'll find that evidence at page 6465. And to round matters off, in late August or early September, being a sensible woman, she had packed her bags, ready to be taken off to Zasavica, in case that should happen, and she described to you an occasion when she saw a truck pull up outside her house, a truck covered with a tarpaulin, and she could hear the voices of people inside, and she describes a policeman going up to her apartment and wandering around outside her apartment, looking for her. She describes to you how she hid behind a garage. The next day, she went and saw Mr. Tadic, who informed her that she and her husband would be exchanged the following day, and you'll find that evidence at page 6479. The Prosecution asks you, invites you, to ask yourselves: Did she have any choice in whether or not she could leave via the system of exchanges, given those series of horrible events that she had been -- that she had witnessed? She didn't leave, if Your Honours please, for family reunification. She left to save her family, her children and herself from a campaign of persecution that was being waged against people such as herself, non-Serbs. Her choice was simply to wait around, be arrested, perhaps wait for the news of her husband's death in custody, to continue leading a life with no future, no safety, none of the normal, decent conditions of life that she had experienced. That was her choice. It was no choice at all. And her plight, in the Prosecution's submission, is exemplary of non-Serbs who were living in Bosanski Samac. In fact, she was one of the lucky ones. She wasn't taken to Zasavica. Consider her account of her life in Bosanski Samac against the words of Mr. Tadic: Not a single one. No one was expelled by force from Samac. All those who left applied to leave of their own free will, and eventually left of their own free will, or returned. No one was kept back in Samac either by force. The Prosecution, if Your Honours please, is not alone in its assessment that the exchanges were involuntary. One of the best possible commentators on the situation that applied in that municipality was one of the defendants, Mr. Simo Zaric. He was interviewed, as you know, in April of 1998, Exhibit P141 ter, and he spoke of the -- one of the exchange occasions that he visited, which was the exchange at a place called Sid, which I think is near Lipovac. He claims that he went there to watch his daughter's family -- his daughter's husband's family leave via the system of exchanges. His commentary makes it absolutely clear that these people had no choice whatsoever. He commented, page 88: "Their departure was in itself something inhumane, but there was absolutely nothing I could do about it." He was asked, page 89: "Sir, would it be fair to say they felt they had no choice but to leave Samac?" Answer: "I think they had no choice. That is my opinion. It is the terrible truth, but it's the truth." And in describing the reasons for his presence there, he said that he was there to be a difficult witness to a great human tragedy, page 89 of his interview. And there you have it from one of the people best qualified to tell you of what was occurring in connection with these exchanges, Mr. Simo Zaric. No choice, terrible tragedy, inhumane. That was the way he saw the humanitarian and humanist work of Mr. Tadic. The -- I mentioned to you earlier that one of the basic planks of the Defence is this notion of family reunification, the notions of family reunification and voluntary return. I want to very briefly deal with family reunification. Put quite simply, the Defence simply say that the humanitarian aspect of the exchanges is illustrated by permitting family reunification. The evidence proves precisely the opposite. The obvious point is that men who were kept in detention for no good reason and then kicked out via the system of exchanges were hardly being reunified with their families. Safet Dagovic testified to you that he watched his family be exchanged until he was the last one left alone in his house. You'll find that testimony at page 7528. He wasn't reunified with his family. He had to spend another year or so fighting with the VRS, forced to fight with the VRS. Ediba Bobic was exchanged in December 1992. Her husband was exchanged in October of 1994. That is hardly an example of family reunification. Witness K was exchanged in November 1992, and her husband, Witness L, was exchanged almost two years later, in October 1994. You'll find that testimony at pages 4361 and 4723. And they are hardly examples of family reunification. The Defence of Mr. Zaric called Andrija Petric. You may recall him. He was the blind Croat. He was taken to the exchange point after having told, he says, the ICRC in prison in Bosanski Samac that he did not wish to go. And the fact that his wife and children were still in Bosanski Samac as he was being bussed off to this exchange point, with no one calling for him from Croatia is hardly an example of family reunification. It's a simple lie, if Your Honours please, and the Prosecution invites you to reject the whole notion that family reunification underpinned the system of exchanges. On the contrary; the evidence is that the system of exchanges was the tearing apart of family life. The other matter that the Defence points you to, to indicate the voluntary nature of the exchange system, was the endorsements on the exchange lists saying people did not have to cross or that they returned, and they ask you to conclude that that indicates that people had freedom, a choice as to whether or not they wished to cross, and that therefore the exchanges were voluntary. The first point that the Prosecution makes to you is the rather obvious point, and that is this: It was at that point that people were truly and honestly and genuinely asked if they wished to cross or not by the fact of the presence of the ICRC at that point. That's the point when they were able to say: No, I don't want to cross. And able to do so in the presence of the ICRC. And that very fact in itself indicates -- goes some way to indicating why it was that some people, notwithstanding the horrors that they had witnessed in Bosanski Samac, felt able to say: No, I don't want to go across. But the fact of those endorsements presented the Defence with an evidentiary problem, because it didn't explain why it was that people who did not want to cross, did not want to go, did not want to leave via the exchange system, would put themselves in a crowded bus and allow themselves to be taken through dangerous, war-torn country to these UN-controlled areas where the exchanges occurred. And so to account for this, the Defence invented the idea that the people who returned were taken there to reassure the Croats that they did not wish to cross. And this makes absolutely no sense at all, in the Prosecution's submission. Places on the buses were, of course, at a premium, and taking people to the exchange points who did not wish to cross over in any event would have taken up valuable space. And secondly, it's at once apparent that the ICRC was in an excellent position to fulfil that role of reassuring the Croats that someone did not wish to cross, if that was truly what the Croats were concerned about. Some of the Defence witnesses, however, failed to establish their essential point, that they, on the contrary, they made no mention of satisfying either the Croats or the ICRC that they did not wish to cross over. I'm referring here to people who returned, who did not cross at the exchange point. Witness DW8/3 was called by Mr. Tadic, and he made absolutely clear that he was taken to the exchange point, where Mr. Tadic supposedly told him he could go or stay, and then he simply remained on the bus. He spoke to no official of his decision to return, other than Mr. Tadic. It fails, then, to provide any evidence of this witness reassuring the Croats or the ICRC, or any other official, that he truly, freely, voluntarily, did not wish to cross. He didn't reassure the Croats at all. You'll find that evidence at 17828 and 17847. The same witness, Andrija Petric, also testified of being taken to the exchange point and being permitted to return. He was a witness called by Mr. Zaric. He told the ICRC that he did not wish to cross, as I've already mentioned to you, back in Bosanski Samac, before he was bussed to the exchange point, back when he was still in his prison, this dangerous, blind Croat who had been imprisoned. He was taken -- in fact, he wasn't bussed, if Your Honours please. He was trucked. This particular witness was taken in a truck to the exchange point. And he again told the ICRC that he did not wish to cross and was permitted to remain at that point. The significance of Mr. Petric's evidence is this: His family, his entire family, was in Bosanski Samac. His wife and kids were in Bosanski Samac. His father-in-law lived in a nearby village. He testified to you that no one had sought him from Croatia, no one asked for him from Croatia, no one -- there was no compelling reason to take him to the exchange point and reassure the Croats that he truly did not wish to leave. On the contrary; he was simply, like so many of the others, just taken in the bus, taken, as I said, in a truck, and, for whatever reason, allowed to return on that occasion. Mladen Borbeli also testified, a Defence witness, also testified of being taken to the exchange, to an exchange point. He described talking to an ICRC official and then being allowed to return. He mentioned nothing in his evidence about reassuring the Croats that he did not wish to cross over. So the evidence of these Defence witnesses negates this assertion, that people who did not wish to cross had to be taken there anyway to satisfy and reassure the Croats that they truly did not wish to cross. And when you look at the evidence in that light, in the Prosecution's submission, it undermines the whole notion that that was the reason why people who did not wish to cross in the first place were taken to the exchange point. If Your Honours please, that's all I want to say to you on the issue of voluntariness of the exchange system. I now want to turn to the involvement of the defendants in the deportation and the forcible transfer process. I'll deal with Dr. Blagoje Simic first. Essentially, his defence is that the exchanges were conducted voluntarily and that people left because of wartime conditions. He claims that the exchanges were conducted under the auspices of the ICRC, and you'll see that at paragraph 349 of his submission, and you can also find that at page 12314 of his -- of the evidence. In addition, however, he argues that the Crisis Staff was not in control of the process of the exchanges involving detainees or civilians, and that it was the army and the police that had control of this process. And you'll find that in his final brief at page 118. As I said, the issue of voluntariness has already been addressed, so this second issue, this second plank of his defence comes to the fore, the involvement of the Crisis Staff. The first and obvious point that needs to be made is that the War Presidency, of which he was the president, itself appointed the Exchange Commission, later in the year. It was their invention, it was their creation. And although it occurred later in the year -- I'll give you the date shortly. Although it was formally created later in the year, the Defence of Dr. Simic explains that this was merely a formalisation of a process of work that had been going on earlier. And Dr. Blagoje Simic says that in his final brief at page 153, when he discusses P83, Exhibit P83, which I'll get to shortly. So yes, the Exchange Commission was created by the War Presidency later in the year, but that just formalised work that had been going on in any event prior to its creation. So that's his position, and the Prosecution doesn't disagree with that. Yes, it was -- there was an Exchange Commission at work, busily exchanging people right from the start. I want to have a look at one particular document briefly, and that is Exhibit P83. And the Exchange Commission was created on the 2nd of October, 1992, so it's October that it came into being, this creature of the Crisis Staff -- of the War Presidency. It's a devastating document for Dr. Blagoje Simic's -- the second limb of his defence, where the Crisis Staff had nothing to do with the exchange system. From that point of view, it destroys his argument. In plain, unambiguous words, it says that the War Presidency took a decision to appoint an Exchange Commission for prisoners and other persons, at its session on the 2nd of October. It makes clear that the composition of the Exchange Commission is dictated by the War Presidency. It shall consist of Velimir Maslic, Simo Nikolic, and Miroslav Tadic. It provides instructions for the work of the Exchange Commission. It requires monthly reports on the exchanges of prisoners to be provided to the War Presidency. And so in that clear, unambiguous language, if you look at P83, taken together with Dr. Blagoje Simic's defence that this body was merely formalising the work that had gone on before, the conclusion is inescapable that the War Presidency, and before that, the Crisis Staff, controlled the exchange process right from the start. The control of the War Presidency over the composition of this body is crucial administrative organ that oversaw the exchanges, facilitated them, is also illustrated by P84, which shows that in November of 1992, again Dr. Blagoje Simic signed a decision appointing Simeon Simic to that Exchange Commission. You can see just how desperate Dr. Blagoje Simic is to distance himself from that document by reading his submission on it. I don't have the reference at the moment. I'll find it briefly. It's in his final trial brief. It's the point at which a whole series of Prosecution exhibits are discussed in detail. And the submission illustrates how desperate he is to avoid the simple and clear implication of the document. The submission is: The mere reporting by one branch of government to another is not sufficient by itself to establish that the latter branch held a superior position or that it in any way governed the actions of the lower branch. P83, if Your Honours please, does not call for mere reporting. P83 indicates that the War Presidency created the Exchange Commission and staffed the Exchange Commission. You can see why Dr. Blagoje Simic is to desperate to avoid the clear, simple, straightforward implications that can be drawn from P83, because it quite simply destroys the argument that the Crisis Staff had nothing to do with the exchanges, in overseeing the exchange work. Of course, the expert on carrying out exchanges, Mr. Tadic, was not shy of admitting Crisis Staff involvement in the exchanges. In his interview on the 27th of March - that's P139 ter - he spoke of how the detention of Serbs in Odzak led to the first exchanges and negotiations, and he commented, at page 57 of that exhibit, talking about exchanges: "At the session of the Crisis Staff, it was decided that I should join the operation because I was from Novi Grad. Simo Zaric, because he was in Trnjak; and Bozo Ninkovic because he was from Dubica." And he made clear that he was talking about events in early May of 1992 leading to the exchanges. Another document that clearly establishes Crisis Staff involvement in the exchanges is Exhibit P99. P99 is a letter written by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac to the federal Executive Council in Belgrade, and it's dated the 17th of May, 1992. Midway through the -- it's a letter. Midway through the text of the letter, this is said: "The Crisis Staff of our municipality has constantly been trying to reach an agreement on the resolution of the issue of the detained Serbs, and in that respect we have proposed that they be exchanged." It goes on to say that their efforts are falling on deaf ears. And this document again makes clear that the Crisis Staff involved itself in negotiations relating to exchanges. If you're in any doubt at all about Crisis Staff involvement in the system of exchanges, then you can look to the view of the Croats -- I'm sorry. Let me withdraw that submission. Exhibit P163 is another document that makes -- that illustrates perfectly clearly just how deeply involved the Crisis Staff was in the exchanges, and not just the Crisis Staff but the Red Cross as well. Mr. Tadic discussed Exhibit P163, at pages 15762 to 66. I'll just pause and diverge there from my main topic for a moment. That passage of evidence from Mr. Tadic, I invite you to revisit. He was asked by Your Honour Judge Williams whether at the time that he created that document he was a member of the Crisis Staff. The question had to come three times from the Bench before you could get a straight answer. And in the Prosecution's submission, is interesting reading from the point of view of the credibility that you attach to the evidence of Mr. Tadic. But in any event, returning to the document P163, it makes abundantly clear that negotiations conducted between the Croatian Red Cross -- negotiations were conducted between the Croatian Red Cross and the Croatian Crisis Staff with their Serb counterparts in Bosanski Samac. In accordance with the agreement reached between the Odzak municipality Red Cross and the Red Cross of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, as well as the Crisis Staffs of the mentioned municipalities represented by Mijo Matanovic from Odzak, and Miroslav Tadic, from Bosanski Samac, it was agreed to carry an exchange of 100 for 100 prisoners in the area of Lipovac in July. Signed by Mr. Miroslav Tadic for the Crisis Staff. So P163 is cogent and compelling evidence, if Your Honours please, of the deep Crisis Staff involvement in the whole system of exchanges, and hence the involvement of Dr. Blagoje Simic in the system of exchanges. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Exhibit D125/3 also illustrates that the Croatian side were under no illusions when it came to the body that they thought they were dealing with when it came to dealing with exchanges. Mr. Tadic produced D125/3, dated the 2nd of May, and that document, which is from the Odzak Crisis Staff, referring to the exchange of one man for another, says that the Odzak municipality may exchange the following persons with the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff. And that's an important document, showing the perspective of the Croatians, who you might think might know something about who they were dealing with when it came to exchanges. If you then add to all of this documentary evidence the evidence of the live witnesses, in particular that of Mr. Todorovic, on Crisis Staff involvement in the exchanges, then you're left with a compelling case against Dr. Blagoje Simic. He was asked in examination-in-chief, page 9165.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nancy Paterson asked you this and you gave this answer. Question by Nancy Paterson: You said that Blagoje had some say on who got put on the list and who wasn't put on the list. Now, I know that exchanges were going on for a period of time, were going on fairly regularly, once a week, once every two weeks, there was an exchange happening. Now, let's talk through how this would work. Would Miroslav Tadic draw up a list and say: This person can go, and that person needs to stay, and you answered: He looked at some lists and I know that he consulted with Tadic. I don't know if he looked at every single list every time. Is that a fair representation of the role of Mr. Blagoje Simic in this exchange process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Blagoje Simic had, of course, signaled his intentions to get rid of the non-Serb population even before the 16th and 17th of April, even before the system of exchanges was put in place, even before Mr. Tadic began his industrious work in that regard. Sulejman Tihic testified of a public meeting just before the takeover, attended by Blagoje Simic, who announced that the municipalities had to be divided along ethnic lines. Orasje and Odzak were to be Croatian; Gradacac was to be Muslim; and Samac was to be Serb. And this announcement was apparently delivered in a "take-it-or-leave-it tone." You'll find that evidence at 1346. Mr. Izet Izetbegovic also spoke about this meeting. He said it was initiated by the SDS and attended by military types. He said it was chaired by Blagoje Simic and that he made the point that Muslims would have to go to Gradacac. He was shown an earlier statement, Mr. Izetbegovic, that is, was shown an earlier statement that he had made on the topic, in which he reported that Blagoje Simic had said that force would be used to bring this about. And he agreed that he hadn't said that in an earlier statement. You'll find that evidence at page 2222 through to 45. And other witnesses also confirm -- give evidence that essentially support that account of events. Dragan Lukac also confirmed that he heard from others who had actually attended the meeting of Dr. Blagoje Simic's pronouncements on how the Croats would have to leave. I want to turn to Simo Zaric. Mr. Zaric's defence seems to be that he was not actually involved in any exchange process, and in particular, that he wasn't involved in negotiations over exchanges, and that he had no authority to negotiate over exchanges. His position is that the all-for-all exchange that came up so clearly in the evidence of Witness Q was in fact actually raised by Witness Q, and another gentleman named Ivo Simic, when they were on the radio. You'll find that he adopts that position at paragraphs 414 to 419 of his closing brief. The Prosecution's submission is that that simply cannot be so. It cannot be so that Witness Q was the man who raised the notion, the idea of an all-for-all exchange. Witness Q, by the time he came to be taken to the communications centre to speak on the radio, had been subjected to a breath-taking round of torture by the paramilitaries. He had been singled out by Lugar in particular and viciously attacked by that man, and was in a bashed and beaten state when he was taken to the communications centre. It is unthinkable, in the Prosecution's submission, that he would be the one who initiated an all-for-all -- the concept of an all-for-all exchange, that he would have had even the slightest liberty to speak about such a topic. Witness Q, on the other hand, places Simo Zaric right in the frame, right in the picture, as the major player, along with Mr. Tadic, in these negotiations. He described essentially four visits to that communications centre, where there was radio communication with the Odzak side. And in the Prosecution's submission, you should have little trouble accepting his evidence as both honest and reliable. It was coherent evidence, it made sense, and it was utterly unshaken in cross-examination on this central issue of the involvement of Mr. Simo Zaric. He made the following points in his evidence in chief: Mr. Simo Zaric was the man who took him from the SUP building to the communications centre, and it was Mr. Simo Zaric who initiated contact with the Croatians. That's at page 11735. It was Mr. Simo Zaric who recommended an all-for-all exchange on both occasions that he was present with Mr. Zaric, and Mr. Zaric replied -- sorry - and on those occasions, it was clear that prisoners were being spoken of. You'll find that evidence at 11737, 11741, and 11749. He said -- Witness Q said, that at one stage, the Odzak side, represented by a gentleman named Ivo Simic, asked if Witness Q could be exchanged, and Simo Zaric replied that Q could not be exchanged until an all-for-all exchange had been negotiated. Now, if you accept this evidence, and the Prosecution plainly submits that you should, then it plainly implicates Mr. Simo Zaric. He's right in up to his neck in negotiations involving the exchange of prisoners and persons, non-Serbs, from Bosanski Samac to a Croatian-held area. It's crucial evidence, in the Prosecution's submission, and it has not been undermined or attacked in any meaningful way by Mr. Zaric. The crucial propositions of Mr. Zaric were put to Witness Q by Mr. Pisarevic, repeatedly. He denied them all. He was asked if Mr. Zaric told him on that first occasion of the first visit to the communications centre -- sorry. Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. He denied propositions from Mr. Pisarevic that Mr. Zaric ever said anything to the effect that he was not on the Crisis Staff, had no authority to negotiate, and was unable to do anything about the issue of exchanges. And you'll find that at 11805 and 11807. The Croatians weren't under any illusion as to the role of Mr. Tadic in the exchanges. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask that we move into private session, because otherwise I believe the witness identity could be revealed. I think that identity could be revealed in this way, and we know why it was requested to have this witness testify in closed session. So if there is going to be reference to this witness, I would kindly ask that we move at least briefly into private session. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I agree. I agree, and if Your Honours please, perhaps it would be wise as well to redact the last four lines of my commentary before -- from lines 16 down to 21, as well. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We are in open session. So you're asking for redaction from line 16 to 21? MR. DI FAZIO: 21, I think that would be safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Protect the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We shall adjourn now and continue our proceedings at 1415 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Maybe Mr. Di Fazio would like to take a look at the transcript. On page 84, line 7. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I meant Mr. Zaric, not the tzar. I didn't go far enough, yes. I can't remember that. It doesn't make sense and in any event, I don't think it matters much. My essential submission is contained in the previous sentence. So I think that takes care of that. Perhaps we can leave it as an inexplicable mistake. One of the -- yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it can be corrected through the audiovisual tape. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Right, Your Honour. I also invite you to look -- I won't discuss this in detail but I invite you to look at other evidence that talks of the involvement of Mr. Zaric in the exchanges, and that is the evidence of -- the evidence of Ivan -- I think it's Cukic. That's from the Rule 71 depositions, page 15 to 18, where he makes it clear that Mr. Zaric was involved in the negotiations over the exchanges. I did plan to address you at some length on the evidence concerning an individual exchange that Mr. Zaric involved himself in, but I think I can get through that a little more swiftly. That was the evidence concerning of exchange of Mr. Izet Izetbegovic. You recall that he testified being taken in his bloodied condition to a room in the SUP building and in the presence of Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic [sic], there were some negotiations concerning exchanges. Mr. Zaric essentially denies that encounter, and you'll see that -- you'll see that at paragraphs 328 to 332 of his closing brief, and he also denied that any such encounter in his evidence, at pages 19 -- pages 19424. The -- all I want to say about this is that if it's a fabrication, then it's a peculiar fabrication on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic. He did not ascribe a particularly major role to Mr. Zaric on this occasion dealing with the exchange. In fact, he said that Todorovic, who was also present, did most of the talking. You'll find that at 2292. So if it's a false implication or false accusation on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic, then it's puzzling as to why he really didn't do the job properly and fully implicate Mr. Zaric in that supposedly false round of negotiation -- exchange negotiations. And it's also puzzling as to why it is that Mr. Todorovic should also speak of the same episode and describe essentially Mr. Izetbegovic being taken to his office to discuss the release of Serbs held in Odzak. You'll find that in his evidence at page 9148. And finally, on Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not mean to interrupt my colleague. I would just like to make the following intervention: I think there's been an oversight by my learned friend and colleague, although that may be his position. He talked about the exchange and about Izetbegovic, and in line 12, page 85 he mentioned Zaric and Tadic. I believe he wanted to make a reference to Todorovic, because the whole submission is about Todorovic and Zaric. I'm not sure if it's the position of the Prosecution that Tadic was actually present at the negotiations when Izetbegovic talked. So I would like to have this point clarified, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I know. Mr. Lukic is completely correct. There's no evidence of Mr. Tadic being there. The encounter is strictly between those three men that I've mentioned, Zaric, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Todorovic. And there's no -- it's not the Prosecution position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. MR. DI FAZIO: And I also remind you of the evidence of Witness A, who told you of evidence that he heard from his spouse of hearing -- of her hearing Mr. Zaric over the radio discussing his exchange in exchange for some pilots. And you'll find that evidence at 10898. So I turn now to the evidence of Mr. -- to the situation of Mr. Tadic relating to exchanges. Now, I don't need to labour all of the evidence here, because it's beyond doubt that he was deeply involved in the exchanges. He was a facilitator, an organising, architect of this final process of persecution. So I don't need to go through all the evidence there. And it's admitted by Mr. Tadic of his -- his deep involvement in the exchanges. So I really only want to address you on two topics relating to him. First is the taking of bribes, and the second is the alleged humanitarian aspect of his work. Firstly, the issue of bribes. You know from evidence in the case and it's uncontested that in 1992 inflation was rampant in Bosnia, and the local currency had become worthless and was becoming even more worthless with the passage of time. Hard currency was at a premium. Deutschmarks in particular were a valued currency, as well as goods, jewellery, and so on. Combine that with large numbers of desperate people who were in the prisons and large numbers of desperate non-Serbs who were in the municipality of Bosanski Samac and the system and situation was ripe for exploitation. Desperate and terrified people will do anything to get out of that sort of situation, and Mr. Tadic was in the perfect position to extract bribes from persons who were, as I said, desperate to exit. Numerous witnesses testified of the connection between Mr. Tadic and the taking of monies. This evidence, of course, is relevant to illustrating his power and control over the system. It demonstrates that that was the perception of people who wanted to pay money to get out, because he was the person they went to offering the money to exit. Firstly, there's evidence of the rumours -- of rumours of payment to -- of bribes to exit Serb-controlled Bosanski Samac. Muharem Kucakic [phoen] talked of it. You'll find that at page 170 of the Rule 71 depositions. Witness DW2/3 -- would Your Honour just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Witness DW2/3 gave -- provided you with evidence of how a relatives of his decided to offer money to Mr. Tadic, and offered a certain sum of Deutschmarks to Mr. Tadic to be permitted to board a bus. You'll find that at 14502. The significant fact, of course, is that they actually went to Tadic. He was a Defence witness, and the evidence was that Mr. Tadic rejected the offer. The Prosecution submission is that it's significant that that witness testified that he even considered going to Mr. Tadic, and bear that evidence in mind when you consider all the other evidence in relation to bribes. Harija Drljacic testified of the notorious fact that Mr. Tadic took bribes to arrange for people to leave. It was an open secret, as she put it. Page 8094. There's the evidence of the witnesses relating to a payment to Mr. Tadic by a person named Sabah Seric. I won't go through that in detail, but I'll just tell you of the witnesses and where you can find that evidence. Witness M testified about that, of how Seric reported that to him, page 5250. Kemal Mehinovic testified how he saw Seric give money to Mr. Tadic in Batkovic, that's page 7472 to 75. A remarkable coincidence you might think, both Witness M and Kemal Mehinovic lived in different countries. Witness C described how Seric told him on the bus when they were leaving Batkovic of having paid money to him, although he did mention that the man who told him that was a Hasan Seric. So perhaps he was mistaken or perhaps he was talking about another man. Jelena Kapetanovic testified of pathetic attempts of her friends to assist her to exit by the payment of bribes not to Mr. Tadic but to Mr. Vasovic, also held a high position within the system of exchanges. I want to simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, can you go back a bit. There is no record of the page number which you mentioned in line -- page 88, line 25. When you talked of Kemal Mehinovic. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. That's at page 7472 to 75. And lastly on the evidence relating to payments to Vasovic you'll find the discussion of Ms. Kapetanovic at pages 10339 to 40. Witness L described an encounter, and I want to quote to you from this particular witness to remind you of what he said. He was talking about a visit to Batkovic, where he was kept for a long time. You may recall Witness L. He was in the Prosecution's submission an outstanding witness, clearly a man of honesty, took his duty to testify here extremely seriously. And the Prosecution submits that you should have no trouble accepting his evidence. He was not, in the Prosecution's submission, a malicious man who would fabricate lies and perjure himself in front of you. He said this, talking about Mr. Tadic at Batkovic: "The two of us exchanged a few words and I said to him: Professor, I'm ready to give some money for helping the Serb army. Please put me on that list. He asked me exactly as he was looking into the ground: Where have you got this money? And I said to him that I haven't got any money on me because the exchange goes through my town every time. This was the ongoing practice. When I go to town, I would borrow money from someone. He said: All right. We'll see. And he continued walking towards the exit of this fenced-off yard. My task was to go back to the hangar. I was awaiting the result." Well, he wasn't exchanged for another two years. So it's -- if you accept this evidence, it shows a -- it's good evidence of powerful control by Mr. Tadic over the exchange process, powerful control by Mr. Tadic over who got to leave via the system of exchanges. In the Prosecution's submission, one of the -- the biggest untruths that you've been told in this case is that the work of the Exchange Commission was humanitarian in nature and that it was the work of humanists. A lot of the Defence witnesses commented in that tone. Velimir Maslic, also called as a witness by Mr. Tadic and a man who played a central role in the exchanges, constantly described his work in the exchanges as humanitarian. Mr. Tadic himself adopted the mantle of humanitarian. Page 15796 he was asked by his counsel in re-examination: Question: "The exchanges in which you took part, was the work related to ethnic separation or was this about bringing families back together? "Very little has been said about the humanitarian aspect of the whole thing here. One of the crucial principles was to bring families back together and this applied to Croats, Muslims, and Serbs equally. Little has been said about that, about how the sick and the wounded were transferred to the other side. All those people who were transferred from one area to another, there was a possibility for them always at a certain point to return to their own place or town. Not everyone was in a position to take advantage of this right, especially Serbs. They did. We had witnesses, my witnesses, who went of his own free will to Gradacac and then he returned and today he has the same job, the same position as he used to have." The Prosecution, with respect, has trouble seeing the humanitarian aspect of the exchange system. You might think that the spectacle of bashed and tortured prisoners being loaded onto buses and trucks and taken to the exchange point somehow does not merit the description humanitarian. You had an opportunity to see the exhausted women and children carrying their few pathetic possessions in that video of the exchange that was shown to you early on in the Prosecution case. You may not think that that spectacle merited the description humanitarian. You may think that the spectacle of a blind Andrija Petric being taken to the exchange point away from his children and his wife was not exactly described -- could not exactly be described as humanitarian. The Prosecution's submission is that it is an appalling misdescription to describe these persecutions as humanitarian and invites you to reject that assertion. That essentially completes my submissions, if Your Honours please, but for one matter, and that is the discriminatory intent required for deportation. I haven't addressed you at length -- as far as -- insofar as the persecutions charge is concerned. I haven't addressed you at length on that. The reason for that is the evidence is overwhelming of a discriminatory intent. Mr. Zaric has already told you how he was aware that the prisoners who were imprisoned were there because -- on ethnic grounds and they were the ones who were going to be exchanged. As far as Mr. Tadic is concerned, it was clear from his deep, profound involvement in the system, that it was non-Serbs who were being ejected by the system of exchanges. And as far as Mr. Blagoje Simic is concerned, it is clear that he knew, must have known, that it was an exchange of us for them; the "us" being the non-Serbs who were held in Bosanski Samac and the "them" being the Serbs who were held in other parts of Bosnia. If Your Honours please, that completes my submissions to you on deportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the three defendants have been charged with the persecution of the non-Serb population of Samac by various means, including the cruel and inhumane treatment of Muslims and Croats through the use of the forced labour system, the wanton and extensive plundering of Muslim and Croat property, and third, the unlawful arrest and confinement of large numbers of non-Serbs on political, racial, and religious grounds. Over the next hour I'll address all three of these issues, beginning with forced labour. Non-Serbs in Samac were forced to work long hours, with no day of rest, without any pay, with little or no food, while they were sick and injured. In the words of Witness K, we were only slaves. And that's at 4635. Non-Serbs were forced to work in dangerous and unhealthy situations at areas on the battlefront, in military or combat areas, in places unsafe for women. Working at the front or at the battle lines was dangerous for non-Serb workers. We have testimony that two men were killed while digging trenches, four were wounded. Nusret Hadzijusufovic at 6879 describes how he felt working during the gunfire. "At any moment, any one of us could have been killed." Another dangerous area for working was Odzak. Odzak was not safe for the women that were working there. Non-Serb women were kidnapped, sexually assaulted, and raped. The record also supports that non-Serbs were humiliated by this work. They were not given assignments that were similar to their occupations, they were embarrassed by certain types of jobs, such as looting. Esad Dagovic said on page 3962 how he felt about looting homes. He said he felt terrible, he felt like a criminal. The evidence further proves that non-Serbs from Samac were forced to work in military capacities. They dug trenches. They built bunkers along the front lines and behind the police station. They mowed grass along the front lines so the snipers would have a good vantage point to shoot. That's at 4286. They built concrete slabs for constructing bunkers. They piled sandbags along buildings and windows to protect soldiers. And they cleaned weapons outside the garages behind the police station. That's at transcript site 3960. Such activities violate the third and fourth Geneva Convention on allowable labour. Articles 50 through 57 on the third convention and article 51 on the fourth convention. The defendant Simic in his brief at page 104, paragraph 338, even concedes that some of the work assignments did not comply with the law. It should further be noted that Muslims and Croats were forced to work -- that some of these people that were forced to work were prisoners. Whether they were prisoners or whether they were undetained civilians. The use of either persons was discriminatory and persecutory. I plan to focus on three areas of labour that were illegal. Military operations, looting and plundering, and the various assignments given to women in Odzak. First, the military assignments. They were dangerous. They violated the Geneva Conventions. They were discriminatory, as only the non-Serbs were digging trenches. Only the non-Serbs were building bunkers. And you get that at page 6880. Defence witness Ljubomir Vukovic agrees with that at page 14683 he says: "The Croats and Muslims dug trenches in the front line which was under the command of the Serb army. And the Serbs dug trenches where the territories of the Muslim and Croat armies were. That's how it was in war." Looting. Non-Serbs were forced to loot homes, shops, businesses, owned and operated by Muslims and Croats. Serb property was not touched. Muslim and Croat property practically disappeared from Samac. We'll discuss this topic a little bit more thoroughly in the next argument when we talk about looting, but looting was an aspect of forced labour. Finally, in Odzak actions such as sweeping of the streets, cleaning, agriculture, generally do not constitute illegal forced labour unless the surrounding facts raise it to that level. Here there were the removal of or kidnapping of young women from the trucks, they were transporting them to and from Odzak, there were rapes, there were sexual assaults, including one woman who was bitten, and that's from the testimony of M at page 5142. There was a lack of protection for the non-Serb women who were forced to work there. Witness K explains at page 4670: "Every day when we went, one, three, or four were victims. Question: Victims of what? Answer: Victims of being taken away and forced sexual intercourse." Based on the conditions, the facts establish illegal forced labour. In fact, you can compare the recent Martinovic and Naletilic judgement at paragraph 269 where they also talk about labour which usually does not constitute forced labour becoming forced labour based on the unhealthy conditions that that work was done in. The forced labour programme discriminated against the non-Serb population in Samac, even the defendant Zaric admits this. The Prosecutor contends that these defendants are responsible for this programme. Let us begin with the defendant Tadic. Tadic oversaw much of the looting process in the municipality of Samac. His civilian protection agency utilised labour to loot homes, shops, and factories. He also assisted in the construction of bunkers. We'll discuss Mr. Tadic's role much more thoroughly in the next section when we talk about looting that went on in Samac. The defendant Simic, the defendant Simic was a member of the Crisis Staff. He was the president. Miroslav Tadic was also a member of the Crisis Staff. The two secretaries of the municipal defence, municipal Ministry of Defence of Samac were Crisis Staff members. The Crisis Staff was responsible for the economy, for the agriculture, public safety, local defence, food, housing, in the words of P128, "all areas of life and work." The forced labour projects performed by the non-Serbs involved these same areas. Further, the municipal Ministry of Defence, which oversaw the forced labour programme, let's look at that. Bozo Ninkovic, its chief was appointed or nominated by the Crisis Staff. His predecessor was appointed or removed by the Crisis Staff. Both of those men served on the Crisis Staff. The Ministry of Defence worked closely with the municipality. In his brief, at page 58, paragraph 233, the defendant Tadic notes that the Ministry of Defence worked with the executive committee. Bozo Ninkovic testified that the Ministry of Defence worked with the municipal government to mobilise workers. That's at page 13373. This is consistent with the testimony of Witness M, that the call-up papers had Crisis Staff written on the bottom; that's at page 5060. The ministry received requests for personnel from the secretary of -- from the secretariat of the economy, page 13372. As you know, the secretary of the ministry of economy is a Crisis Staff appointment. At harvest time, the executive committee of Samac established a plan of action. The secretariat of economy and local commissioners implemented and further developed that plan and the Ministry of Defence provided labour. Even the chief of police participated in the illegal forced labour assignments. If you look at the sentencing judgement of Stevan Todorovic at paragraph 42 and page 9029 in his transcript. This was all one municipal system coordinated by Blagoje Simic and the Crisis Staff, that persecuted the non-Serb population. And finally, with regard to Mr. Simic, we've had testimony from -- or we have a statement from Simo Zaric indicated that Simic participated and profited in the looting. Zaric's liability -- Zaric's liability is different from the others. Zaric was part of the persecutory system. He was part of the military civilian council in Odzak. He was part of that and he was -- and he participated in that to make Odzak inhabitable. And in order to do that, they had to use the forced labourers. They had to use those non-Serb labourers from Samac. The civilian military council requested them and orchestrated their work. He was aware of the allegations of rape. He states that in P141 ter at 9596. And he was aware of the looting. In that same document he states that at page 92 through 94. And what does he do? He continues to work in the system. He remains a member of the civilian military council. He participated in a system where non-Serb women were being used in a discriminatory manner to do labour. Now, the defendants raise a number of defences or responses that can be dismissed quickly. Tadic, paragraph 248 and 249. He states, "Although people had no choice to work, no one was forced to go." If we look at the transcript, we see Witness K, who was forced to go to Odzak and Korenica. They forced her out of her house barefoot and into a truck. That's at pages 4724 to 25. Also, who would dare to refuse the labour knowing that there were prison camps where beatings and tortures were occurring on a daily basis? You can see Nusret Hadzijusufovic make a similar statement at page 6923. Tadic at paragraph 254 says, "The work force was comprised of Muslim and Croat males since all the Serb males were in the military." There's no proof of this allegation. And also ask yourself: What about the five to ten thousand Serb refugees that came into Samac? They couldn't work. What about Serb women? They couldn't sweep the streets. They couldn't clean. They couldn't help out in Odzak. Tadic further states at paragraphs 265 to 268: "The fact that some people were paid means that the Prosecutor cannot prove that the workers were not paid." Witness after witness, members of the court, testified that they were not paid. The fact that a select or privileged few, or a select or privileged group of Muslims and Croats were paid does not prove that the majority were paid. And if you want to compare something to that, we can look at the Martinovic and Naletilic judgement at paragraph 267, page 94, which also rejected this same argument, where the fact that a few people received some benefits doesn't mean that everyone received benefits. Tadic argues at paragraphs 293 to 303 not to believe Nusret Hadzijusufovic. He must be lying. Common sense, however, tells you that he isn't lying. There's no allegation of any bias, prejudice, dislike, hostility, hatred towards Mr. Tadic. There's no showing of any incentive that he had to lie. Further, he got most of his information from one of the labour force coordinators. Tadic finds that odd, but that isn't odd, because the coordinator and Nusret Hadzijusufovic had a long-standing relationship. Prior the war, Dzevad Celic was Nusret's manager at that same factory, and that's at page 6897. He was the person who Nusret could talk to. He called Nusret to his office for a meeting at page 6929. Furthermore, the fact -- Tadic indicates well, Nusret didn't know everyone's official position. Nusret was basically working as a slave. He was given a job each day and told to do it regardless of whether he had the proper clothes, regardless of how he felt, regardless of if he was sick, regardless of if he was injured. He didn't see any piece of paper with any hierarchy or list of positions of who held what positions in Samac. Tadic finally argues that Nusret has to be wrong where he said he was sent by Tadic to build those slabs that were used to make the concrete barriers to be used at the front lines, those concrete bunkers. He said that only the military commanders were involved in constructing these bunkers. And this argument here rests on the testimony of Bozo Ninkovic and Djordje Tubakovic. So let's review their testimony. Bozo Ninkovic, the man who worked for informational services but did not know about the Crkvina massacre. He only heard rumours about it two to three months later. That's at page 13531 to 33. Bozo Ninkovic claims that he did not know what his labourers were doing for the military, at pages 13390 through 391. He claims that he didn't know that certain labourers were killed or injured until sometime later, again at pages 13390 through 391. He even claims that he never learnt of the names of those killed until months later. What we have here is the assistant to the chief of information who is completely uninformed of what is happening in Samac --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
