utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic's testimony is not worthy of belief. The other witness who testifies about this is Djordje Tubakovic. He was the witness who gave the testimony about Tadic right here on the witness stand, which was in direct conflict with his recently sworn and signed statement. We argue that his testimony is unreliable on any matters relating to Tadic, based on his prior conduct. But even if the Court wants to believe their testimony, Tadic, we submit, is still involved. Common sense tells you that when you need -- when you have to choose who to assign to work, you have to call someone. You have to call someone you trust. There was only one telephone in that building where the work assignments were given out, and that was in civilian protection. The military commanders had the option of calling the non-Serb coordinators or speak with Miroslav Tadic, who regularly used the labourers. Miroslav Tadic, a former assistant to the commander of the 4th Detachment. Miroslav Tadic, a member of the Crisis Staff. Miroslav Tadic could be trusted to select this personnel. Nusret Hadzijusufovic's evidence is consistent with the circumstances in Samac. Finally, Tadic claims at paragraph 256 that there was no discrimination in the assignments. Proof of the discrimination comes from three Defence witnesses. Defendant Zaric admitted that the labour system was discriminatory, at 141 ter, at page 95. Muharem Kucakic [phoen], a fireman, who testified under Rule 71, at pages 95 and 104, 105, tells you that non-Serb firemen were sent to the front lines to dig trenches. He doesn't tell you that Serb firemen had to do it. Non-Serb firemen were sent to the front lines to dig trenches. Ljubomir Vukovic, who we have previously mentioned. Who does he say had to dig the trenches in the Serb-controlled areas? The Muslims and Croats. Consequently, the defence case does not support Miroslav Tadic's claims. The defendant Simic claims that he had no influence over the civil protection or the defence ministry, at pages 20 through 21 of his brief. He argues that he and the Crisis Staff were not involved with the local Ministry of Defence or the work labour programme. The defendant Simic wants us to believe that he was the Crisis Staff president that reigned but did not rule. Rather, the evidence supports that the defendant Simic and the Crisis Staff oversaw the system of persecution in Samac. The forced labour programme furthered the system. It made life unbearable for the Muslims and Croats. Forced labour was used to dismantle the homes and businesses of the Muslims and Croats and seize their property. It left them with no reason to stay or return to Samac or Odzak. Forced labour was also used to ensure the liveability and the survival of the Serbian municipalities of Samac and Odzak. In fact, the best example that we can use is Odzak, to show this one system. The Crisis Staff sends Savo Popovic and Simo Zaric to Odzak to help out and rebuild the city. The municipality - I'm sorry - the municipal Ministry of Defence of Samac immediately transfers their work assignments to Odzak. A civilian military council is established in Odzak, and Savo Popovic becomes its president. He remains a member of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency. When Popovic needs help, who does he go to? From his own testimony, he goes to the Executive Board and the municipal Ministry of Defence, pages 16285 and 286. Every enterprise in Samac had to help, page 16286. When workers were needed in Odzak, the Ministry of Defence from Samac supplied them on a daily basis. And the labourers were utilised in the same manner as they were in Samac. During this time, Savo Popovic continued to report on the situation in Odzak to the Crisis Staff. That's at P142 ter at 127. It was all one system. And the defendant Blagoje Simic was in charge of it. Therefore, the Prosecutor contends that this system persecuted the non-Serbs of Samac and used forced labour as a tool to do so. I'd like to continue on with the mass looting and plundering of Muslim and Croat property. It was committed with a discriminatory intent to persecute the non-Serbs. The mass looting was used to destroy the homes of Muslims and Croats, to take away any means of income, to rob and steal their property; consequently, the non-Serbs had no property worth staying for in Samac and nothing to return to. Esad Dagovic saw his economic prosperity collapse with the looting of the pizzeria where he worked. At page 3957 he says: "The pizzeria was a place where I earned my daily bread and I could see that this tower of my source of income was being toppled in all this looting." Looting and plunder were committed on a mass scale, victimising the non-Serb property. The people doing it were the soldiers, paramilitaries, civilians, police officers, and local officials. They were the ones that were involved in this programme of theft. Now, during war, certain property may be requisitioned. Certain property may be legal to seize, based on the situation with the army. In Samac, however, it was nothing more than plain theft and robbery that occurred. It's obviously from what was taken. Electronic equipment, rugs, furniture, currency, jewellery, gold and silver, pianos, tobacco curing equipment and household items. All these thefts were used to dismantle houses. They took the plumbing fixtures, the heating systems, wiring, windows, doors, window and door frames, roofs, floors, and all available construction material. All that was left of the Muslim and Croat houses was a shell. Muhamed Bicic described the condition of his house at page 3039: "There is nothing in the house, no doors, no windows, no water pipes or cables, electricity cables, or anything like that, or parquet floors, let alone the furniture and all other things that were in it. That has all disappeared, and the house was devastated, completely destroyed." It was the Muslim and Croat property that was targeted. Several witnesses describe going from house to house in Croat villages, in a town or in a -- the section of a town where the Muslims and Croats live, going to the Muslim and Croat houses in the town of Samac or Odzak to steal property. We have that from Nusret Hadzijusufovic, 6907 to 15; Esad Dagovic, 3950 to 55; Witness M, 5052 to 5056; and Witness K, 4634 to 35. The homes and businesses of the Serbs were not looted. We had several witnesses, Esad Dagovic, Witness M, and Nusret Hadzijusufovic tell us that. Witness M notes that there were signs indicating that a certain house was owned by Serbs and they would not loot it. He says that at 5098 to 5101. Now, Defence witness Dusan Gavric corroborates this, saying that he even put a sign on his house saying it was a Serb house at 17350. The result of this extensive looting of Muslim and Croat property was the -- pretty much the destruction of the property of the Muslim and Croat community in the municipality of Bosanski Samac and parts of Odzak. In Exhibit P127, the military command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of the Republika Srpska describes the looting by the paramilitaries and locals, at page 2. With the blessing of those who brought them in -- with the blessing of those who brought them in and those who had sent them, they engaged in unheard of looting of private and socially owned property, which was systematically transferred to Serbia and perhaps other parts of Yugoslavia. They were soon joined by local criminals, which made the overall moral picture of this war even more complete and clear. Who was responsible for this massive looting and plundering? Simic and the Crisis Staff. Marko Tubakovic testified at the Rule 71 hearing that the brigade command, the 2nd Posavina Brigade command, was concerned that the looting of the non-Serb property was ordered by the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, at page 231. This testimony is consistent with the 13 signatories document, P127, with the military command states at page 8: "Organised centres of power on both municipal and broader Republika Srpska level are behind the organised looting." Now, Stevan Todorovic testified that the Crisis Staff tacitly approved of the looting, at 9188. He later adds that the paramilitaries looted as part of their war booty, page 9461. Now, this is significant where he mentions for the first time war booty. And it's significant because two Prosecution witnesses provide similar evidence. Witness N claims that he learned from the guards and relatives that Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic made a deal with the paramilitaries concerning the looting in the town. That's at 6361 through 67. Esad Dagovic provides similar testimony. While speaking with some paramilitaries outside doing forced labour, they tell him everything that they looted and plundered were theirs, at page 3926 through 27. This evidence becomes even more interesting when one considers the circumstances of the paramilitaries' return to Samac later in 1992. If you recall, one of the first issues to be resolved was the amount of booty that the paramilitaries could take for helping in the Orasje operation. They demanded 50.000 dinar per person in cash and booty. Now, Colonel Beronja in the statement to the military prosecutor, P115, states that the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, and the chief of police of Samac urged him to bring the paramilitaries back. Beronja later says he was against paying this exorbitant pay of 50,000 D-marks [Realtime transcript read in error "dinars"] per person but he says at page 1 the Samac officials kept telling him to do it. Exhibit P115, page 1. This situation here demonstrates that the Serbian paramilitaries were little more than mercenaries or gunmen for hire. There was not a lot of cash available in Samac or in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were -- they were allowed however, because there wasn't a lot of cash to take, they were allowed to take whatever they wanted. They did this in Samac. They planned to do it in Orasje. The only inference from this is that they had standing orders to loot wherever they went. On page 105, line 6, it says dinars. It should be D-marks. Deutschmarks. Same on page 2, line 2 of 105. Sorry about that. The Crisis Staff and Blagoje Simic are also responsible, since they assisted the civilian protection agency and the municipal Ministry of Defence with the lootings. All goods were stored at public warehouses in the municipality. We know that from Nusret Hadzijusufovic, pages 6906 to 6908. They were storing goods at Samac Trans, at Agropromet, and other warehouses had. All municipal agencies worked together in the system of persecution. Police chief Stevan Todorovic even admits his involvement in the looting, at page 9029 and paragraph 47 of his sentencing judgement. In fact, if you recall, when we talk about looting and looting of buildings, in Exhibit P169 are the notes of a military commander who attended a meeting in Odzak. And discussed at that meeting by Savo Popovic, with Blagoje Simic present, was the looting of building materials of non-Serb housing. And I suggest when you look at that, you see that it was a regular plan by these people to loot building materials from non-Serb housing, because at that meeting, Savo Popovic says, at page 2 in P169: In the Croatian villages, some houses remained intact and building material should be taken from them, while the rest should be levelled to the ground. The Crisis Staff, however, was required to prevent looting. Exhibit P128, paragraphs 3 and 13, describe the role of the Crisis Staff in protecting property, both private and public. When Serb property, however, was looted, actions were taken. The defendant Simic sent a letter to the Republic president, to the Defence minister, to General Mladic and the 1st Krajina Corps commander, complaining that -- complaining of soldiers stealing from "a Serbian house owned by a Serbian soldier." And that's at D62/1, on page 1. D62/1, page 1. When non-Serb property was looted, no letters were sent, no decisions were issued. And if you ask why the defendant Zaric tells us, in P141 ter, paragraphs -- pages 92 to 94. Why were no letters sent when non-Serb property was being looted? Let's see what Zaric says. It was the Crisis Staff that organised the looting and allowed it to occur. As a result, they had no incentive to stop it. They had no incentive to prevent it. The defendant Tadic, he was also a member of that Crisis Staff. In this manner, he joined them with overseeing the system of persecution. He held a powerful position in Samac being on that Crisis Staff. If you recall, while he testified, he talked about one day a paramilitary named Zvjezdan and a few other paramilitaries came with Zvjezdan and went to Tadic's home to take a statement from him. And at page 15415, how does Tadic respond to them? With this phrase: Do you know who I am? And in this manner he let the paramilitaries know that he was not one to fool with, that he was a powerful person in Samac. But more important, Tadic participated in the looting. Nusret Hadzijusufovic explains that he was sent to loot property on Tadic's orders. He went out with civilians. They selected parts of houses of buildings that they wanted. Nusret removed them, transported them back to Samac, and installed them. Doors, windows, plumbing fixtures. He testified that he seized all sorts of construction building materials, from shops, stores, and houses. He also looted stores and houses in the surrounding Croat villages of Samac, and he tells us no receipts were ever left, no inventory was ever made. They didn't even know who owned the property. Two of Tadic's witnesses from the civilian protection staff corroborate much of Nusret Hadzijusufovic's testimony. Zeljko Volasevic admits that the civil protection agency used Muslim and Croat workers waiting in line downstairs. He says first they got permission from the Ministry of Defence, and then they contacted Beg Kapetanovic and Dzevad Celic to assign the workers. That's at page 17770 to 771. And what did they use these workers for? One, housing and building repairs; two, to obtain housing and construction materials, such as doors, bricks, boards, and window frames. At 17771 to 72. This is just what Nusret Hadzijusufovic tells us. He says he was sent to loot Muslim and Croat homes, yards, shops and businesses for construction materials and brought them back to Samac. That's 6905 to 6908. He testified that he was assigned to go out with local Serbs. They told Nusret that they made their request to Miroslav Tadic and he approved their requests. They went out and searched for those specific housing materials they needed they were removed and installed in Serb homes. Ljubomir Vukovic testifies for the defendant Tadic. He also admits that the civilian protection agency used Muslim and Croat workers. They, Vukovic and Tadic, would ask Beg Kapetanovic and Dzevad Celic for some of the labourers. They would be sent to perform building, housing -- building and housing repairs. And that's at pages 14667 to 71. Where did they get these materials, such as the windows and frames, the doors, the roofing materials, the bricks or tiles for repairs? Nusret Hadzijusufovic, his testimony corroborated by Zeljko Volasevic, and our common sense tells you that these were the looted materials. Even Tadic in his brief at paragraph 316 admits that they were using these labourers. He states that his agency, like all other institutions, were beneficiaries of the work obligation programme, and he cites the testimony of Vukovic and Volasevic. Therefore, even the defendant Tadic's evidence supports his participation in the looting and plundering of Muslim and Croat property. The defendant Zaric, his involvement is different from the others. He describes the Crisis Staff's role in the looting, but claims not to be involved. Zaric, however, was part of this system of persecution. He had positions with the 4th Detachment, served as chief of national security for approximately a month, was assistant to the president of the civilian military board of Odzak. In these roles, he saw what was occurring. He knew all about this. He knew that the system persecuted and discriminated against the non-Serbs, but he continued to work in that system and he assisted in its work. Finally, I'd like to move on to the last issue, which are the arrests and confinement of the non-Serbs. Witness Petar Karlovic, a Defence witness, testified that the madness started on the 16th and 17th of April. That's at page 18447. Including in his description of the madness were the arrests of the Muslim and Croats. This Chamber has heard testimony that hundreds of Muslim and Croat civilians were arrested, detained, and confined in the Serbian municipality of Samac. A few Serbs were arrested but were released shortly thereafter. But the Muslim and Croat civilians were arrested and held at various locations, including the police station, the Territorial Defence building, the primary school, the high school, the Crkvina warehouse, and in Zasavica. They held or detained men, women, children, the elderly, a blind man, and a priest. While these people were detained, they were subjected to beatings, torture, sexual assault, extortion, murder, and the extraction of their teeth. We need not discuss what happened to these people, since the defendants do not contest the cruel and inhumane acts that were perpetrated on these prisoners. The Prosecution submits that the charges used to arrest and detain these people were false. The real reason for the arrest of the Muslims and Croats were their ethnicity. The command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of the Republika Srpska criticised the arrests in Samac in P127 at page 2, stating: "The massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims followed, without any criteria." On page 4 of that same exhibit, they criticise numerous arrests on trumped-up charges. Police inspector Vladimir Sarkanovic testified at page 16560, that there were certain arrests which were made for no reason at all. But I suggest there was a reason for these arrests. It was the removal of the Muslim and Croat political and business leaders, it was removal of the possibility of opposition from the non-Serbs, it was the removal of Muslim and Croat people to establish a bank of persons who could be used for the trade, who could be traded for non-Serbs. And how do we know this? Several Defence witnesses testified that the Muslims and Croats of Samac were being arrested and detained on the basis of their ethnicity. Let's begin with the defendant Zaric, at page 19811.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't deny, do you, having heard their moving and harrowing tales what happened to them, what many non-Serbs -- that many non-Serbs were persecuted in Bosanski Samac in 1992 and 1993. You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying that. It's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't deny, do you, that hundreds of Muslims and Croats were arrested in Bosanski Samac only based upon their ethnicity? You don't deny that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not denying that. I agree with you. Marko Tubakovic, who was a signatory of P127, one of those military commanders who signed that document, also criticised the discriminatory nature of the arrest, and he explained why they drafted that document at page 230 of the Rule 71 hearings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's because the Posavina 2nd Brigade command was concerned that the civilian authorities, that's the Crisis Staff and War Presidency, were ordering the detention of Muslims and Croats for ethnic reasons only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. We could not justify anyone being detained without reason, without grounds, being detained or mistreated, and we criticised such practices as something which shouldn't happen. The command of the brigade did, that is. That is why we wrote this report." Witnesses Teodor Tutnjevic and Petar Karlovic testified that Muslim and Croat civilians were being sent to Zasavica because of their ethnicity. Tutnjevic was at pages 17495 to 497. Karlovic at 18440. Finally, Defence witness Jovo Savic describes the discriminatory policies that were being implemented in Samac against the non-Serb population, and he does this at pages 17165 to 17166.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the other members of the command had grave concerns about the arrests, the rounding up of non-Serbs, the torturing of non-Serbs in the detention facilities, the isolation of non-Serbs, and the actions of the Crisis Staff. That's a fair summary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you had seen, these people were pursuing policies against the non-Serbs that could only be described as discriminatory, that is, arresting them, detaining them, torturing them, because they were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As a result of these persecutory and discriminatory policies, hundreds of non-Serb civilians of Samac were arrested, detained, and confined based on their ethnicity. Let's consider who is responsible for this. Blagoje Simic, we submit, was involved in the arrests and detentions. The basis of this is as follows: One, he ordered the local SDA party -- Sulejman Tihic -- I'm sorry, he ordered him to surrender. And that's at pages 1369 and 1372. Simic ordered his surrender by telephone. Two: Police chief Dragan Lukac testified that he was told that he was being arrested on orders of the Serb Crisis Staff and he asked who was in charge of this Serb Crisis Staff, and they said Blagoje Simic. And that's at page 1662. Now, Simic denies this order. There is no reason, however, for Dragan Lukac to lie about this. If Dragan Lukac wanted to lie about the situation, he could have manufactured all sorts of incriminating admissions coming from Simic, but he didn't do that. I suggest that his limited comment concerning the arrest must then be true, as it is not consistent with manufactured evidence. In addition, the Crisis Staff issued and Blagoje Simic signed Exhibit P71, which orders the isolation of the Croat population. Todorovic testified that Blagoje Simic admitted that he issued that document. The defendant Zaric saw the document in three offices at the police station in Samac and noted that the signature looked just like Simic's. That's at pages 19755 to 56 and 19799. Zaric also noted that the decision was made by the Crisis Staff in response to the imprisonment of the Serbs of Odzak, and that's at P141 ter at 72. Now, the defendant Simic tries to state that he did not issue this document and that it didn't come from the Crisis Staff. First he claims, in paragraphs 308, that his fellow Crisis Staff members denied the legitimacy of the document. Common sense tells us that they deny it because they would be incriminating themselves in war crimes if they admitted that they passed and issued that document. These people weren't going to come forward here and say: Yes, I did it and I'm guilty. It just doesn't happen. He also tries to state that it can't be their document because it's typed in Latin script, while the Crisis Staff decisions were in Cyrillic script. However, if you look at the documents relating to the decisions of the Crisis Staff, you'll notice that some of them are typed in Cyrillic script and some, which Simic does not contest the legitimacy of, such as P85 and P86, are typed in Latin script. In addition to that, Mitar Mitrovic testified here, who is the secretary to the Crisis Staff, that he believed the Crisis Staff had a Latin script typewriter, and that's at page 18751. The Defence further claims that Professor Aleksic confirms that it's not Blagoje Simic's signature. However, if you look at Professor Aleksic's report, he indicates that he was not able to analyse the signature, since the document that he had to analyse or examine was not legible enough. So he could not make any determination with regard to that signature. Against these weak arguments, we have the independent testimony of Zaric and Todorovic, which includes an admission from the defendant Simic. Other testimony was introduced concerning the Crisis Staff as presiding over -- as presided over by Blagoje Simic and its involvement in arrests and detentions. Todorovic testified that the Crisis Staff approved the arrests from day one, at page 9114. That the Crisis Staff was involved in the release or exchange of large groups of important persons, at page 9118 to 19. He testified that the Crisis Staff was aware of the establishment of the prison camps, at pages 9137 to 39. Now, this testimony is supported by the record. We know from Zaric, when there was a discussion of an all-for-all exchange, he had to get Crisis Staff approval. He says that in P141 ter, at pages 79 and 80. We also know that in a letter from Blagoje Simic, that -- I'm sorry - we also know that Blagoje Simic wrote a letter concerning the plight of the Serbs in Odzak, and he mentions that the Crisis Staff was trying to work out an exchange. That's at page 98. Finally, we know that the municipal buildings -- that municipal buildings were being used to house these prisoners. These weren't defence buildings. These were the schools, municipal buildings within the town of Samac. Therefore, it's our contention that Blagoje Simic participated personally and with the Crisis Staff in the unlawful and discriminatory arrests of Muslims and Croats. Tadic. The defendant Tadic was also involved in the arrests and detention. He was involved as a member of the Crisis Staff, a member who attended meetings, a member who voted, from his own testimony. Tadic used these prisoners. He used them to trade for the Serbs of Odzak. These prisoners were his pawns in the exchange or human trading process. He took bribes from various people to get an earlier exchange. Those people who couldn't pay the bribes, like Hasan Subasic remained in prison. Zaric was also involved in this discriminatory system. He was interrogating these prisoners. He was obtaining information from the police about their investigations. He was using these prisoners for propaganda purposes. The Court will have the chance to review again that video, P16, and the transcript, and to see the flagrant use of propaganda, how that so-called documentary was used. Todorovic indicates that Zaric was involved in the arrests by providing intelligence information to him, and that's at pages 9994 and 10113 tells us this statement is true. Who else other than Zaric the local chief of intelligence would have the information at the beginning of the takeover as to who was involved in the arming. Zaric knew that because that was Zaric's business. Now, how does the Defence respond to this? Blagoje Simic claims he was not aware of the mass arrests of the Muslims and Croats. He was not aware of the isolation of the Croats. He was not aware of the beatings, the tortures, the murders. He was not aware that Zasavica was being used as a prison camp. How could anyone not know what was happening in this very small town of Samac? How could the person who coordinates all functions of life not know what was happening in this very small town of Samac? This defence of see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil, is not worthy of belief. Rather, there was a persecutory system and everyone participated. Todorovic and the paramilitaries arrested, Zaric admitted that the Crisis Staff gave Lugar authority to arrest and detain persons, at P142 ter, at 75. The Crisis Staff gave Lugar authority to arrest and detain. The Crisis Staff ordered the isolation of Croats. Police and military implemented this. Municipal schools were used to detain these prisoners. Tadic used the prisoners to exchange for Serbs. Zaric interrogated the prisoners for the army. And we have testimony that Blagoje Simic, on a few occasions, visited the high school and TO. It was all one large persecutory system, and everyone had a part or a stake in it. The defendants try to argue that many of these people were lawfully arrested on firearms and insurrections charges. The problem with that was that it was all a sham. A priest, a blind man, elderly women, children, elderly men were not possessing arms. They were not revolting against the state. The process was a sham. The arrests were made without warrants, on little or no proof, and the prisoners were beaten immediately upon arrival. The arrests were made on a selective basis. Even though all three ethnic groups illegally possessed weapons, it was only the Muslims and Croats that were arrested. It was only the Muslims and Croats that were interrogated. It was only the Muslims and Croats that were beaten and tortured. It was only the Muslims and Croats that were murdered. It was only the Muslims and Croats in those facilities that were raped. It was only the Muslims and Croats that were told they were not guilty but were still held in confinement. Even the Defence witness Naser Sejdic who was involved in arresting Muslims and Croats admits that the arrests and interrogations were discriminatory, at pages 17561 and 17562. On page 17561, the question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is simply this: The fact that the Serbs were not being arrested for doing what the Croats and Muslims were doing, that is, arming themselves, from what you saw, meant that those arrests of non-Serbs were discriminatory. The arrests were made on discriminatory grounds, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Serbs were not being arrested. Only Croats and Muslims who had weapons. More on page 17562:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that non-Serbs were interrogated after their arrest, which you have agreed to was on discriminatory grounds, because they were non-Serbs, the fact of their interrogation itself was discriminatory too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They interrogated only Muslims and Croats. Now, with regard to the insurrection charges, arrests on this basis were also a sham. Vladimir Sarkanovic testified that he was a lawyer, that he was a criminal investigator, that he was investigating the charges at the police station in Samac. He testified he was investigating those charges on behalf of the Republika Srpska government concerning armed revolt against the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that's at 16662 -- I'm sorry 16622 to 23. Your Honour, would you like me to stop here and just finish up in five or ten minutes tomorrow morning or would you like to go on for another five or ten minutes and finish today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I hope the interpreters can bear with us for five or ten minutes so that we can complete that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's important. He was investigating on behalf of the Republika Srpska government armed revolt against the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, he's investigating Muslims and Croats for revolting against their own new nation, according to his testimony. This demonstrates the absurdity of the situation, since it was the Serbs who were revolting, but no Serb was ever arrested or questioned on this issue. Further proof that the arrests and the interrogations were a sham concern the actual statute relating to armed revolt or insurrection. The armed revolt or insurrection charge was removed from the BiH Criminal Code in early April, and if you look at Exhibits P186 and 187, you'll see that the armed revolt charge, paragraph 124, was removed. Consequently, investigator Sarkanovic was investigating a crime that didn't even exist, based on his own testimony. Therefore, we maintain that the majority of Muslims and Croats were arrested only on the basis of their ethnicity, that the weapons and insurrection charges were a pretext for illegal arrests based on their ethnicity. And for those few people that there were grounds to arrest, the process itself was so corrupt that those arrests were also illegal. I thank the Court, as well as the interpreters, for their patience. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I believe we have approximately 30 minutes or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 35 minutes left for tomorrow to cover sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because we did take that time in the morning when we started. We shall adjourn now. The Trial Chamber thanks the interpreters and the supporting staff for bearing with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
